abstract: Uniform color spaces and color-difference formulae rest on visual data obtained almost entirely with surface samples and conventional displays, whose primaries confine the measurements to a limited chromaticity range. The highly saturated region of color space is therefore the least measured part of human color perception, at the moment when quantum-dot, microLED, and laser displays have begun to operate inside it. Closing this gap requires stimuli more saturated than any fixed-primary device can produce, together with the stability and uniformity demanded by visual experiments. We present an acousto-optic colorimeter built for this purpose. A four-channel acousto-optic tunable filter selects narrow spectral components from a supercontinuum laser over the calibrated range of 443--660~nm, with measured linewidths of 1.37--3.20~nm; the wavelength and radiance of every component are set electronically, so the primary set itself becomes an experimental variable. A compact diffuser--light-pipe homogenizer combines the selected components into a uniform observation field, and spectral feedback stabilizes their intensities. The calibrated primary set covered 95\% of the area enclosed by the CIE 1964 $10^{\circ}$ spectral locus in the $x,y$ chromaticity plane. The calculated maximum luminance reached 1406~cd\,m$^{-2}$, with 328~cd\,m$^{-2}$ available at the gray Robertson chromaticity. Across an 18-mm observation field the mean spatial $ΔE_{00}$ difference was 0.913, and five Robertson color centers reproduced under continuous feedback gave mean target errors of 0.34--1.26~$ΔE_{00}$ over 10-min intervals. The instrument thus delivers calibrated, uniform, and stable highly saturated stimuli, and is intended to extend the empirical basis of color-difference measurement into the region where data are still absent.
one_liner: A four-channel acousto-optic colorimeter produces calibrated, stable, highly saturated optical stimuli beyond fixed-primary displays.
why_it_matters: It provides instrumentation for measuring human color perception in saturated regions now accessible to quantum-dot, microLED, and laser displays.
detailed_summary: The instrument uses four acousto-optic tunable-filter channels to select narrow components from a supercontinuum laser over 443-660 nm. Wavelength and radiance are electronically controlled, while a diffuser-light-pipe homogenizer and spectral feedback provide uniform, stable fields. It covers 95% of the CIE 1964 10-degree spectral-locus area, reaches calculated luminance up to 1406 cd/m2, and maintains low spatial and temporal color errors.
main_result: The authors demonstrate a calibrated colorimeter delivering uniform, feedback-stabilized, highly saturated stimuli across a broad chromaticity range.
application_angle: The system can support new color-difference data and calibration standards for advanced laser, microLED, and quantum-dot displays.

title: Entanglement Swapping Scheduling for Quantum Repeater Chains under Decoherence during Classical Communications
abstract: First-generation quantum repeaters are essential in distributing entanglement over long distances since they could mitigate losses in optical fiber. Repeaters split the total distance into shorter, easier to generate links. Then, entanglement swapping establishes long range entanglement by performing local measurements at the repeaters and heralding their results. In this work, we develop an analytical model that estimates the impact of decoherence during heralding for a given protocol. Furthermore, we identify a competition between two phenomena: as repeater count increases, so does entanglement generation, but the additive impact of memory decoherence on final entanglement rate increases too. Therefore, we find that an optimal number of repeaters exists. These findings could lead the design of future quantum networks, both in the inter-repeater distance and swapping timings.
one_liner: An analytical model quantifies how heralding-time decoherence changes optimal entanglement swapping schedules in repeater chains.
why_it_matters: It identifies the repeater-count and timing tradeoffs that future long-distance quantum networks must optimize in real memories.
detailed_summary: The paper models first-generation quantum repeater chains where memories decohere during the classical communication needed to herald swapping outcomes. It captures the competition between shorter elementary links, which improve entanglement generation, and accumulated memory decoherence, which lowers the final entanglement rate. The analysis predicts an optimal number of repeaters and links that optimum to swapping timing and inter-repeater spacing.
main_result: The authors derive an analytical framework showing that memory decoherence during heralding produces an optimal repeater count.
application_angle: The model can guide quantum-network layout choices, including node spacing, memory requirements, and entanglement-swapping schedules.

title: Squeezed light from a semiconductor amplifier
abstract: The possibility of generating light in a squeezed quantum state during saturated light amplification in a semiconductor amplifier is theoretically analyzed. Due to four-wave mixing process during amplification, weak components of the spontaneous emission of the medium with symmetric frequency shifts relative to the strong amplified wave acquire the quantum properties of two-mode squeezed light. The squeezing of quadrature components occurs in the range of frequency shifts of several GHz ($\sim$ the inverse relaxation time of the charge carrier density) and can reach 10 dB or more under optimal conditions. The formation of a two-mode squeezing phase facilitates the observation of the squeezing effect, in which a strong wave, playing the role of a local wave, exhibits quadrature noise suppression without additional homodyne detection.
one_liner: Theory predicts two-mode squeezed light generation during saturated amplification in a semiconductor optical amplifier.
why_it_matters: A chip-compatible amplifier source of GHz-band squeezing could simplify quantum photonic links and sensing readout architectures.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes saturated light amplification in a semiconductor amplifier, where four-wave mixing couples spontaneous-emission components symmetrically detuned from a strong amplified wave. Under optimal conditions, quadrature squeezing can reach 10 dB or more over frequency shifts of several GHz, set by carrier-density relaxation. The strong amplified wave can act as a local wave, enabling observation of quadrature noise suppression without a separate homodyne setup.
main_result: The authors theoretically show that saturated semiconductor amplification can generate observable two-mode squeezed light with potentially >10 dB squeezing.
application_angle: The scheme suggests compact semiconductor sources for squeezed-light photonics, quantum communication, and noise-reduced optical sensing.

title: Broadband Telecom Entanglement from an All-Fiber Type-0 Sagnac Source
abstract: We demonstrate a compact, practical all-fiber source of non-degenerate telecom-band polarization-entangled photon pairs assembled from off-the-shelf components. The compact fiber-integrated architecture is designed to be affordable, straightforward to assemble and align, and compatible with existing optical-fiber infrastructure. Photon pairs are generated through type-0 spontaneous parametric down-conversion in a pigtailed periodically poled lithium-niobate waveguide embedded in a Sagnac interferometer. At 0.5 mW pump power, quantum-state tomography yields a Bell-state fidelity $F_{Φ^-}=0.850$, purity $P=0.836$, and concurrence $C=0.782$. A separate CHSH measurement gives $S=2.3301\pm0.0075$. The measured Bell-state fidelity is sufficient for the reconstructed polarization state to support qubit teleportation above the classical fidelity limit under ideal protocol operations. Analysis of the density matrix shows that approximately 96.7% of the population remains in the desired $|HH\rangle$-$|VV\rangle$ subspace, with a normalized coherence of approximately 0.86. A residual relative-phase offset indicates that local phase compensation could increase the Bell-state fidelity to approximately 0.8865. We further characterize the brightness--quality trade-off and obtain a corrected pair-rate slope of $(0.918\pm0.040)$ Mcps mW$^{-1}$. The broadband emission and fiber interfaces offer a route to multiuser entanglement distribution through off-the-shelf multichannel wavelength-division multiplexers with passbands matched to the signal and idler wavelengths.
one_liner: A compact all-fiber Sagnac source generates broadband telecom polarization-entangled photon pairs from a pigtailed PPLN waveguide.
why_it_matters: Fiber-integrated, off-the-shelf telecom entanglement sources lower the barrier for deployable quantum-network and WDM multiuser links.
detailed_summary: The paper demonstrates a non-degenerate telecom-band polarization-entangled photon-pair source using type-0 SPDC in a pigtailed periodically poled lithium-niobate waveguide inside a fiber Sagnac interferometer. At 0.5 mW pump power, tomography gives Bell-state fidelity 0.850, purity 0.836, and concurrence 0.782, while a CHSH test yields S = 2.3301 +/- 0.0075. The density matrix retains about 96.7% population in the HH-VV subspace, and phase compensation is projected to raise fidelity to about 0.8865.
main_result: The source produces telecom-band polarization entanglement with Bell violation and a corrected pair-rate slope of 0.918 Mcps mW^-1.
application_angle: Its fiber interfaces and broadband output make it well suited to practical entanglement distribution over existing telecom and WDM infrastructure.

title: Total-field atomic magnetometry using an elliptically-polarized frequency-modulated light beam for geomagnetic-field applications
abstract: We investigate an all-optical scheme for high-sensitivity measurements of the Earth's scale magnetic field ($B$). The scheme is based on the Bell-Bloom technique with frequency-modulated light. A single elliptically polarized light beam is used both for pumping the alkali-metal atoms and probing Larmor precession of their spins under the external magnetic field. In contrast to many other high-sensitivity magnetometry schemes based on nonlinear polarization rotation of the light, the proposed approach enables the observation of magnetic resonance via changes in the light-beam ellipticity parameter. The approach has been validated in experiments with a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser, irradiating a $0.125$ cm$^3$ cesium vapor cell filled with a buffer gas. In the current experimental conditions, the achieved sensitivity is estimated at $220$ fT/$\surd$Hz under $B$$\,\approx\,$$50$ $μ$T, while the shot-noise floor corresponds to $\approx\,$$20$ fT/$\surd$Hz. The bandwidth is estimated at $\approx\,$$1$ kHz. The proposed simple and robust single-beam scheme is well suited for miniaturization and is therefore particularly promising for the development of compact, highly sensitive, low-power-consumption atomic magnetometers for a wide range of applications in the geomagnetic field.
one_liner: A single elliptically polarized frequency-modulated beam enables compact Bell-Bloom atomic magnetometry at Earth-field scale.
why_it_matters: The single-beam cesium scheme points toward low-power, miniaturized total-field magnetometers for geomagnetic sensing outside the lab.
detailed_summary: The work studies an all-optical Bell-Bloom magnetometer using one elliptically polarized frequency-modulated beam for both pumping and probing alkali spin precession. Instead of relying on nonlinear polarization rotation, the resonance is detected through changes in the beam ellipticity parameter. Experiments with a VCSEL and a 0.125 cm^3 buffer-gas cesium cell reach an estimated 220 fT/sqrt(Hz) sensitivity near 50 microtesla, with a shot-noise floor near 20 fT/sqrt(Hz) and about 1 kHz bandwidth.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates total-field atomic magnetometry at geomagnetic fields with 220 fT/sqrt(Hz) sensitivity and kilohertz-scale bandwidth.
application_angle: The simple optical layout is attractive for compact, robust, low-power magnetic sensors used in navigation, geophysics, and field monitoring.

title: Classical Verification of a Remote Quantum Processor via Degenerate Concordant Computations: An Application to Randomness Generation
abstract: A client who rents a cloud quantum processor cannot easily tell whether the bitstrings it receives came from a quantum device. Certification by random circuit sampling runs on present hardware, but scoring each returned sample costs the client time $O(2^n)$. We give a protocol in which the client scores each round in time $O(n)$, built on degenerate concordant ensembles. When a concordant state has a degenerate spectrum, every concordance-preserving gate factorizes as $G_t=U_tP_tB_tU_{t-1}^\dagger$, and the block factor $B_t$, which commutes with the state, cancels from the ensemble while entangling each pure component. The client holds a secret parity whose cosets are the degenerate sectors of every layer, so that it builds the circuit and predicts the ensemble with one inner product per layer. The secret never leaves the client. Inputs are sent uniformly at random, and the client attaches to each round, in its own bookkeeping, the eigenvalue of that input in the hidden state; both verification statistics, an input--output agreement test and a weighted collision test, then compare the server's samples with the non-flat output distribution of the concordant computation. We prove completeness, client efficiency, and soundness in an ideal model in which the compiled circuit reveals nothing about the secret, and we show that the secret must stay hidden: a classical server that holds it passes. For the explicit construction we prove that the single-qubit symmetry test used in efficient simulations of concordant computation fails on non-product inputs with unbiased marginals, and we measure that the local-basis finder of Cable and Browne halts on every layer we tested, that the transmitted component saturates the maximal Schmidt rank, that the circuit is not Clifford, and that matrix-product spoofers are rejected. Soundness of the explicit construction is stated as a conjecture.
one_liner: A client-efficient protocol verifies remote quantum processors using degenerate concordant computations with O(n) scoring per round.
why_it_matters: Efficient verification is a practical bottleneck for cloud quantum hardware, especially when clients cannot classically score random-circuit samples.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes a remote-processor verification protocol based on degenerate concordant ensembles, where the client keeps a hidden parity defining degenerate sectors. The client can build circuits and predict the ensemble using one inner product per layer, enabling O(n) scoring instead of exponential-time sample evaluation. The protocol includes input-output agreement and weighted collision tests against non-flat output distributions, with ideal-model completeness and soundness proofs; soundness of the explicit construction is left as a conjecture.
main_result: The authors give an O(n)-per-round classical verification method and test an explicit non-Clifford construction against several spoofing strategies.
application_angle: This could make quantum-cloud certification and certified randomness generation more practical for clients with limited classical compute.

title: Multi-time advantage for certifying quantum coherence
abstract: Non-classical dynamics in open quantum systems can be hidden in temporal correlations that are invisible to standard state- and channel-based tests. We define coherence for multi-time quantum processes and show that access to intermediate times can reveal coherence absent from all corresponding pairwise channels. Incoherent processes are fixed points of dephasing on all input and output spaces, and their coherence is quantified by relative entropy. As a proof of principle, we use an Ising model in which all three pairwise channels are incoherent while the full three-time process remains coherent. We observe this multi-time coherence on a superconducting quantum processor using a coherence witness and full process tomography.
one_liner: Multi-time process access reveals quantum coherence hidden from all pairwise state and channel tests.
why_it_matters: Temporal diagnostics can expose non-classical dynamics missed by standard benchmarks, improving characterization of open quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The authors define coherence for multi-time quantum processes, treating incoherent processes as fixed points of dephasing across all input and output spaces and quantifying coherence by relative entropy. They construct an Ising-model example where every pairwise channel is incoherent but the full three-time process remains coherent. A superconducting quantum processor is used to observe this effect with a coherence witness and full process tomography.
main_result: The experiment certifies multi-time coherence in a process whose corresponding pairwise channels appear incoherent.
application_angle: The method adds a sharper diagnostic for memory effects and hidden coherent dynamics in noisy quantum processors.

title: Synthesizing free-electron wave functions by stimulated near-field interactions
abstract: Stimulated electron-optical-near-field interactions imprint a coherent, phase-coherent modulation on the wave function of a free electron, of which the free-space dispersion subsequently converts into a train of attosecond density peaks. Light thereby becomes a tool for synthesizing the electron wave function itself, setting when, where, and how narrowly the electron density concentrates. Here we study photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM) to gain control over that synthesis in two stages: first for a single PINEM interaction, whose design parameters we obtain in closed form, and then for multiple PINEM interactions acting in parallel, which extends the control across space and time. The design rules follow from decomposing the propagated density into temporal harmonics, which we classify into three: (i) the arrival time of the attosecond train, fixed by the optical phase of the coupling; (ii) the distance at which the train forms, set by diffraction at the point where all classical trajectories converge; and (iii) the pulse duration, fixed by the imprinted energy spread. We evaluate these parameters for a scanning-electron-microscope (SEM) configuration at 10~keV, where the compression completes within tens of micrometers from the interaction region, with results 20% better than previous approaches. Letting the electron then interact with several spatially separated near fields in parallel, normal to the trajectory, each pathway carrying its own coupling strength and optical phase, we show that retaining or erasing which-path information changes both the propagated density and the measurable energy spectrum, the latter providing in turn a measure of the mutual coherence of the driving fields. These results establish PINEM as a quantitative synthesis tool for free-electron wave functions in compact, low-voltage electron microscopes.
one_liner: Design rules for PINEM interactions synthesize attosecond free-electron density trains in compact low-voltage microscopes.
why_it_matters: Coherent electron-wavefunction shaping can improve ultrafast electron microscopy and enable compact probes of optical near fields and coherence.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes photon-induced near-field electron microscopy as a controlled way to imprint phase-coherent energy modulation on free-electron wave functions. It derives closed-form design parameters for a single PINEM interaction, linking optical phase to arrival time, trajectory convergence to formation distance, and energy spread to pulse duration. For a 10 keV SEM configuration, compression occurs within tens of micrometers and is reported to improve by about 20% over prior approaches; parallel near-field interactions also probe mutual coherence through the energy spectrum.
main_result: The authors provide quantitative design rules for generating attosecond electron density trains and controlling multi-path near-field interactions.
application_angle: This supports compact ultrafast electron microscopy and coherent electron-optical instrumentation at low acceleration voltage.

title: Perfect Bound States and non-Markovian Dynamics for Imperfect Giant Atoms in a Semi-Infinite Waveguide
abstract: Bound states in structured reservoirs require exact interference conditions and are therefore sensitive to imperfections in the coupling geometry. In this paper, we study a two-level giant atom coupled at multiple points to a mirror-terminated semi-infinite waveguide. The exact atom-photon bound state requires both cancellation of the outgoing radiation amplitude and dispersive matching to the atomic detuning. Generalized delay-equation dynamics, continued-pole spectra, and real-space photon fields verify this criterion for coupling-strength, position, and coupling-phase imperfections. For representative realizations, retuning restores one-, two-, and three-root responses after strength errors and one- and two-root responses after position errors. The specified position-imperfect three-root configuration fails because its $2π$ root is no longer dark, consistent with a $58.77\%$ spectral mismatch. Ensembles of 1000 realizations at each error amplitude show near-unity target-state recovery for strength errors, unity recovery of the specified one- and two-root targets but no three-root recovery for position errors, and no nontrivial exact recovery for independent phase errors. Optimized phase-imperfect responses instead retain finite linewidths. Root matching with realization-dependent control retuning therefore constitutes a compensation procedure, rather than generic passive robustness against arbitrary disorder.
one_liner: Retuning can recover exact atom-photon bound states for some imperfect giant-atom waveguide couplings, but not arbitrary disorder.
why_it_matters: Understanding imperfection tolerance is essential for engineering waveguide-QED hardware with giant atoms and long-lived photonic states.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes a two-level giant atom coupled at multiple points to a mirror-terminated semi-infinite waveguide. Exact atom-photon bound states require both outgoing-radiation cancellation and dispersive matching to the atomic detuning, which the authors test using delay-equation dynamics, continued-pole spectra, and real-space fields. Retuning restores target responses under many coupling-strength and position errors, but independent phase errors retain finite linewidths and a specified position-imperfect three-root case fails due to spectral mismatch.
platform_or_system: Giant atom in a semi-infinite waveguide
main_result: The work identifies exact recovery conditions and shows when control retuning compensates coupling-strength or position imperfections.
application_angle: These criteria guide robust design and calibration of waveguide-QED devices for quantum photonic memories and interfaces.

title: A 3D-Printed GHz Microwave-Resonator Paul Trap for Electron Confinement and Millisecond Spin-Qubit Coherence
abstract: We report a 3D-printed microwave-resonator Paul trap that operates at the GHz frequencies required for electron confinement while preserving an open geometry suitable for laser access and imaging ion Coulomb crystals. The resonator exhibits moderate quality factors of approximately 1000, enabling large confining electric-field amplitudes at low input power, and is in good agreement with finite-element-method (FEM) predictions despite manufacturing imperfections, which we experimentally characterize. The validated FEM model is then used to calculate the electromagnetic fields in the trapping region. These field distributions, together with surface-roughness measurements, are incorporated into a model of electron spin-qubit decoherence to estimate the coherence time. Our analysis predicts that electron spin-qubit coherence times on the order of 10 ms should be achievable under the assumption that motional heating is dominated by Johnson noise, making such systems relevant for quantum information processing. The method of obtaining the coherence time is applicable to any electron Paul trap.
one_liner: A 3D-printed GHz Paul-trap resonator is validated for electron confinement with predicted millisecond spin-qubit coherence.
why_it_matters: It points toward manufacturable, optically accessible electron traps that could support compact spin-qubit hardware.
detailed_summary: The paper reports a 3D-printed microwave-resonator Paul trap operating at GHz frequencies suitable for electron confinement while retaining open optical access. Measured resonator behavior, with quality factors around 1000, agrees with FEM simulations despite characterized manufacturing imperfections. The validated field model and surface-roughness data are used to estimate electron spin decoherence, predicting coherence on the order of 10 ms when Johnson-noise heating dominates.
main_result: The authors demonstrate a manufacturable GHz resonator trap design and predict electron spin-qubit coherence times of about 10 ms.
application_angle: Low-power, optically accessible electron traps could become practical building blocks for trapped-electron quantum information processors.

title: Harnessing Post-selected von Neumann Measurements to Strengthen Entanglement and Quantum Signatures in Coherent States
abstract: We investigate how post-selected von Neumann measurements modify the nonclassical properties of two-mode entangled coherent states (ECSs). From the conditional pointer state, we characterize squeezing, photon statistics, intermode correlations, entanglement, fidelity, and post-selection probability. Anomalous weak values with moderate coupling enhance squeezing, antibunching, sub-Poissonian statistics, intermode correlations, and bipartite entanglement, while fidelity captures the crossover from weak perturbation to strong distinguishability. These results demonstrate post-selection as a tunable approach to engineering ECSs.
one_liner: Post-selected von Neumann measurements are shown to enhance nonclassical signatures in entangled coherent states.
why_it_matters: It gives a tunable measurement-based route for engineering optical states with stronger squeezing, antibunching, and entanglement.
detailed_summary: The work analyzes two-mode entangled coherent states after post-selected von Neumann measurements through the resulting conditional pointer state. It tracks squeezing, photon statistics, intermode correlations, fidelity, post-selection probability, and bipartite entanglement. Moderate coupling with anomalous weak values can strengthen squeezing, antibunching, sub-Poissonian statistics, and entanglement, while fidelity marks the transition from weak perturbation to strong distinguishability.
main_result: The study shows that post-selection can tune and enhance multiple nonclassical properties of entangled coherent states.
application_angle: Measurement-conditioned optical-state engineering is relevant for continuous-variable photonics, quantum metrology, and optical information processing.

title: Quantifying the fidelity of a quantum memory
abstract: Quantum memories are key ingredients for future quantum networks. Developing methods for their certification is therefore an important, yet challenging, problem. In this work, we present a general framework for certifying quantum memories and quantifying their performance in an operational and efficient manner, taking advantage of developments in the theory of quantum channels. We start by giving a pedagogical introduction to these concepts and tools and illustrate their natural application to quantum memories. Specifically, we quantify the fidelity of a quantum memory via the notion of average channel fidelity, which can be estimated precisely in an experiment via a finite set of probe states forming a so-called $2$-design. We then present a number of witnessing techniques for certifying this quantity, and show that it gives access to other important properties of the channel, such as its dimensionality and its capacity to transmit quantum information. We consider mostly a simple prepare-and-measure scenario, but discuss also the case of an entanglement-based setup, as well as a semi-device-independent approach. Finally, we apply these methods to a solid-state quantum memory experiment, certifying an average channel fidelity of 98.6%. Our certification methods can be readily applied to other quantum devices, such as fibers, transducers and gates.
one_liner: A channel-fidelity framework certifies quantum memories and is applied to a solid-state memory with 98.6% average fidelity.
why_it_matters: Efficient, operational certification is essential for comparing memories used in quantum networks and repeaters.
detailed_summary: The paper develops an operational framework for certifying quantum memories using average channel fidelity, estimated experimentally with a finite set of probe states forming a 2-design. It also presents witnesses that connect the certified fidelity to channel dimensionality and quantum information transmission capability. The methods are discussed for prepare-and-measure, entanglement-based, and semi-device-independent settings, then applied to a solid-state memory experiment.
main_result: The authors certify an average channel fidelity of 98.6% in a solid-state quantum memory experiment.
application_angle: The protocol can support practical benchmarking of memories, fibers, transducers, and gates in quantum-network deployments.

title: Entanglement Sudden Death: Eberly's Work and the Limits of Local Dynamics
abstract: Entanglement sudden death (ESD), explored through a series of works by Yu and Eberly, supports the notion of entanglement vanishing abruptly and completely at a finite time, even when the underlying open-system dynamics remain smooth. In this article, we revisit the development of ESD from bipartite origins to genuine multipartite entanglement. We first illustrate the canonical mechanism of ESD with two independently damped qubits, for which the concurrence vanishes at a finite time while populations and coherences remain nonzero. We next present our results on multipartite entanglement for generalized GHZ states under depolarization. Global and independent local depolarizing dynamics can be chosen to produce identical reduced evolution for every individual qubit, yet they yield different genuine-multipartite-entanglement sudden death times, whose ordering can reverse with the initial state. For N-qubit GHZ states, this distinction becomes asymptotically stronger since the ESD time scales as 1/N under independent local depolarization, whereas under global depolarization it approaches a finite value in the thermodynamic limit. Echoing a central lesson of Prof. Eberly's work, we report the lifetime of multipartite entanglement is not fixed by the local dynamics, but rather depends on the evolution of the joint quantum state.
one_liner: The paper revisits entanglement sudden death and shows multipartite lifetimes are not determined by local dynamics alone.
why_it_matters: It clarifies limits of local-noise intuition for preserving multipartite entanglement in many-qubit systems.
detailed_summary: The article reviews the canonical two-qubit mechanism where concurrence vanishes at finite time despite smooth open-system evolution. It then analyzes generalized GHZ states under global and independent local depolarization that can produce identical single-qubit reduced dynamics. Despite matching local behavior, the genuine multipartite entanglement sudden-death times differ, and their ordering can reverse depending on the initial state.
main_result: The work shows that multipartite entanglement lifetime depends on joint-state evolution rather than being fixed by local reduced dynamics.
application_angle: This matters for diagnosing entanglement robustness in noisy many-qubit sensors, processors, and networked quantum states.

title: Efficient Learning of Structured Fermionic States under General Quadratic Evolution
abstract: We prove that unknown pure fermionic states prepared from disjoint-branch fixed-particle-number blocks can be reconstructed after general quadratic evolution, including pair creation and annihilation. For a fixed particle cap per block, adaptive or nonadaptive single-copy Gaussian measurements yield classical input and circuit descriptions with prescribed fidelity and confidence, using polynomial resources in system size and inverse infidelity. The adaptive procedure has the sharper copy guarantee. Connected quartic correlations and a covariance-compatible commutant identify the hidden blocks; local states are recovered from fresh measurements or a predetermined bounded-degree moment table. Stable branch recovery gives valid preparation descriptions. Neither particle-number conservation nor block homogeneity is required; no lower bound on branch weights or covariance gaps is assumed. A certified variant returns a passive preparation whenever one exists within the promised family, without advance membership information. On the full Gaussian orbit of paired magic states, quartic measurements alone suffice, with an explicit bound converting observable error into state error.
one_liner: The paper proves efficient reconstruction of structured fermionic states after general quadratic evolution using Gaussian measurements.
why_it_matters: Efficient learning of fermionic quantum states can aid characterization of simulators and photonic or matter-wave platforms with fermionic encodings.
detailed_summary: The authors prove that pure fermionic states built from disjoint-branch fixed-particle-number blocks can be reconstructed after general quadratic evolution, including non-number-conserving terms. With a fixed particle cap per block, adaptive or nonadaptive single-copy Gaussian measurements recover classical circuit descriptions with polynomial resources. The method identifies hidden block structure through connected quartic correlations and a covariance-compatible commutant, with certified variants for passive preparations and paired magic-state orbits.
main_result: The paper establishes polynomial-resource learning guarantees for a broad family of structured fermionic states under quadratic evolution.
application_angle: Such learning tools can improve validation and debugging of fermionic quantum simulators and state-preparation devices.

title: Observing the magic Mpemba effect in localized dynamics on a digital quantum computer
abstract: The Mpemba effect challenges the intuition that states closer to equilibrium must relax faster. We ask whether an analogous magic-ordering reversal can occur in the generation of quantum magic (nonstabilizerness), a key resource for universal quantum computation: can a state with less initial magic overtake one with more and reach its asymptotic value sooner? Here, we uncover interaction-induced dephasing as a distinct mechanism for this magic Mpemba effect, requiring neither transport nor conventional thermalization. For tilted product states in an interacting $\ell$-bit model, a random-phase analysis predicts a reversal of the magic ordering: states with less initial magic attain higher saturated magic, independent of their spatial pattern. Exact simulations of the $\ell$-bit model and localized spin chains further show that these states also saturate earlier. We observe both features on IBM superconducting quantum processors. An effective $\ell$-bit implementation accesses long dephasing times at fixed circuit depth by encoding time in gate angles, while a microscopic spin model exhibits the reversal universally across initial patterns in the localized regime but only selectively in the ergodic regime. These results establish interaction-induced dephasing as a route to anomalous quantum-resource relaxation beyond transport-driven thermalizing dynamics.
one_liner: IBM quantum processors observe a magic Mpemba effect where initially less-magic states can saturate to higher magic sooner.
why_it_matters: It experimentally probes relaxation of nonstabilizerness, a core resource for universal quantum computation, on real hardware.
detailed_summary: The study proposes interaction-induced dephasing as a mechanism for a magic Mpemba effect in localized quantum dynamics. For tilted product states in an interacting l-bit model, analysis and simulations predict that states with lower initial magic can reach higher saturated magic and do so earlier. The authors observe both effects on IBM superconducting processors using an effective l-bit implementation with time encoded in gate angles, and also study microscopic spin models across localized and ergodic regimes.
main_result: The authors experimentally observe reversal in magic ordering and earlier saturation for selected states on digital quantum hardware.
application_angle: Understanding anomalous magic relaxation can inform benchmarking, resource generation, and control strategies for noisy quantum processors.

title: High-Fidelity Inter-Species Rydberg Gates with Two-Photon Driving
abstract: Recently, neutral atom arrays have become known for their promising potential in quantum information processing. High-fidelity entangling operations are typically achieved by exciting atoms to high-lying Rydberg states through two-photon processes. To improve the performance of these systems at the hardware level, dual-species strategies have been applied to enhance readout, error correction, and reloading in neutral atom systems. However, the influence of laser crosstalk arising from two-photon excitation for dual-species systems has remained largely unexplored in the literature. Here, we develop a model that incorporates the influence of crosstalk in inter-species Rydberg gates with two-photon driving. We demonstrate that the influence of this crosstalk can be suppressed to arbitrarily small levels through appropriate gate design, with gate fidelities greater than $99.8\%$ achievable with conservative experimental parameters in the near-detuned case of an $^{85}$Rb/$^{87}$Rb system. We also outline how this fidelity can be further enhanced through improvements to the Rydberg excitation.
one_liner: Models and designs high-fidelity two-photon inter-species Rydberg gates for dual-isotope neutral-atom arrays.
why_it_matters: Dual-species neutral atoms need entangling gates that tolerate laser crosstalk, a key hardware issue for scalable readout, reload, and error correction.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a model for two-photon inter-species Rydberg gates that explicitly includes laser crosstalk between species. For a near-detuned 85Rb/87Rb implementation, the authors show that appropriate gate design can suppress crosstalk to very small levels. Conservative parameters still yield predicted fidelities above 99.8%, with further gains possible through improved Rydberg excitation.
main_result: The work predicts inter-species Rydberg gate fidelities exceeding 99.8% despite two-photon laser crosstalk.
application_angle: It supports dual-species neutral-atom processors where one species can aid readout, reloading, or error correction without sacrificing gate quality.

title: An efficient variational polaron master equation for non-Markovian spin-boson dynamics: Transformed initial states and general observables
abstract: We investigate the effects of initial states on the dynamics of a quantum spin-boson model using an efficient variational polaron master equation approach. The transformation of a factorized system-environment initial state into the variational polaron frame introduces inhomogeneous terms in the master equation, essential for accurately describing non-Markovian dynamics beyond the weak coupling regime. To efficiently account for these effects, we formulate the dynamics in an extended auxiliary Liouville space, converting the resulting integro-differential equations into coupled ordinary differential equations. We further introduce a simplified variational polaron technique for computing the time evolution of expectation values of general observables, including those that do not commute with the polaron transformation, overcoming a major limitation of previous approaches and enabling the unified treatment of coherence and population dynamics. The effects of transformed initial states generated from arbitrary factorized initial states are systematically characterized through expectation values and trace-distance analysis, providing insight into the associated bath-relaxation dynamics over a broad range of tunneling amplitudes, temperatures, and coupling strengths. Comparison with the weak-coupling master equation reveals a delay phenomenon associated with multi-bath-quanta processes, pronounced at intermediate coupling strengths and tunneling amplitudes. We further show that coherent superposition initial states induce stronger nonequilibrium effects than localized states, with inhomogeneous terms playing a crucial role in the short-time dynamics. The proposed formalism applies to both undriven and resonantly driven spin-boson models, providing a computationally efficient framework for open quantum-system dynamics with arbitrary factorized initial states and general physical observables.
one_liner: Extends variational polaron master equations to transformed initial states and general observables in non-Markovian spin-boson dynamics.
why_it_matters: Efficient open-system modeling is important for interpreting solid-state, molecular, and photonic quantum devices beyond weak coupling.
detailed_summary: The paper formulates variational polaron-frame dynamics for arbitrary factorized initial system-bath states, including the inhomogeneous terms generated by the transformation. It maps the resulting integro-differential problem into coupled ordinary differential equations in an auxiliary Liouville space. The method also handles observables that do not commute with the polaron transformation, enabling unified treatment of population and coherence dynamics in driven and undriven cases.
main_result: The authors provide a computationally efficient variational-polaron master-equation framework for arbitrary factorized initial states and general observables.
application_angle: The approach can help model decoherence and bath-memory effects in quantum emitters, molecular systems, and photonic environments where weak-coupling master equations fail.

title: Valley transitions during spin shuttling in Si/SiGe heterostructures
abstract: Valley excitations are considered one of the biggest challenges for a coherent spin shuttling in Si/SiGe heterostructures. In this work we theoretically investigate the valley dynamics during spin shuttling in a Si/SiGe heterostructure by considering a two-level system given by the two low-lying valley states of the mobile quantum dot. We assume that the electron is initially in the valley ground state and analyze the evolution of this state during shuttling. We find that, depending on the shuttling velocity, the system can be in three distinct regimes. In one of these regimes, the quantum information is preserved even in the presence of the valley excitations, allowing for coherent spin shuttling independently of the shuttling distance. This regime is obtained for a shuttling velocity of tens of m/s, a desired regime where dephasing mechanisms, such as spin-valley hotspots and spatially varying spin splitting, can be suppressed. This result is in accordance with recent experimental work that obtained a high spin shuttling fidelity after a fast and long shuttling. We also propose strategies based on the Partial Landau-Zener model to enhance the valley shuttling fidelity, which was found to be much more efficient than previously proposed strategies based on the standard Landau-Zener model.
one_liner: Analyzes valley-state transitions during electron spin shuttling in Si/SiGe quantum-dot heterostructures.
why_it_matters: Reliable spin transport is a core requirement for scalable silicon quantum processors with separated qubit zones and shared interconnects.
detailed_summary: The work models the two lowest valley states of a mobile quantum dot during spin shuttling in Si/SiGe. It identifies three velocity-dependent regimes and finds a regime at tens of meters per second where spin information can remain preserved even with valley excitations. The authors connect this to recent high-fidelity long-distance shuttling experiments and propose Partial Landau-Zener strategies to improve valley shuttling fidelity.
main_result: The study predicts a fast-shuttling regime where coherent spin transfer can be maintained independently of distance despite valley dynamics.
application_angle: It informs operating speeds and pulse strategies for silicon spin-qubit architectures that move electrons between memory, logic, and readout regions.

title: Teleportation of a programmable gate
abstract: Alice and Bob each have a qubit, and they would like to perform a two-qubit gate on them with the assistance of Charlie. The action of this gate depends on a parameter, which either Charlie knows, will receive later as classical information, or is encoded in a program state. We discuss both the case in which Alice and Bob send Charlie their qubits, which he entangles with his state, and the case where Alice and Bob use teleportation to entangle their states with Charlie's state. All of these procedures depend on the ability of Alice and Bob to apply local correction operations that depend on the results of measurements that Charlie makes, and we discuss under what conditions such operations are possible.
one_liner: Studies how Alice and Bob can implement a parameterized two-qubit gate with Charlie using entanglement and teleportation-style corrections.
why_it_matters: Programmable nonlocal gates are relevant to distributed quantum processing, delegated operations, and communication-assisted hardware architectures.
detailed_summary: The paper considers protocols where Alice and Bob want a two-qubit gate whose action depends on a parameter known to Charlie, supplied later classically, or encoded in a program state. It compares schemes where qubits are sent to Charlie with schemes where teleportation entangles Alice and Bob's states with Charlie's resource. A central technical issue is when Alice and Bob can apply local correction operations conditioned on Charlie's measurement outcomes.
main_result: The work characterizes conditions under which a programmable two-qubit gate can be teleported or mediated by a third party with local corrections.
application_angle: It clarifies primitives for networked quantum processors where gates may be delegated, programmed remotely, or assembled from communication resources.

title: Cost of Delay for Post-Quantum Migration: Putting Classical and Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Risk on One Ordered List
abstract: Organisations deciding which assets to migrate to post-quantum cryptography first, and how that work competes with a backlog of classical findings, lack a common unit: post-quantum scores are dimensionless and quantum-only, while classical risk is annualised loss. We express both threats as a cost of delay in currency per year on the same asset. The quantum term is the rate at which deferring migration commits irreversible harvest-now-decrypt-later loss, computed from required confidentiality duration, recordable traffic share and data turnover, using a quantum-arrival law fitted in closed form to published expert anchors. A competing-risks factor couples the two terms so the same loss is not counted twice. We prove that the construction is not a weighted sum of a classical and a quantum score, give a dominance threshold on the classical hazard that is independent of asset value, and show that the induced order is optimal for sequencing work under constant loss rates. We verify the implementation by simulation, adaptive quadrature and a second implementation. On four public systems with parameters assumed from public documentation, the quantum term reorders the asset list beyond input uncertainty for one system only (signal-to-noise 1.36 against 0.14-0.46), moves specific long-lived, quiet, recordable assets decisively, and otherwise changes magnitudes. Asset value and turnover explain 73-91% of the uncertainty in the quantum term; the arrival date explains 3-17%. The case studies are illustrative and are not validated against outcomes.
one_liner: Introduces a currency-per-year cost-of-delay metric for prioritizing post-quantum migration alongside classical cyber risk.
why_it_matters: Organizations need actionable migration ordering for harvest-now-decrypt-later threats, not just abstract quantum-risk scores.
detailed_summary: The paper expresses classical cyber risk and post-quantum harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure in the same unit: cost of delay per asset per year. Its quantum term uses confidentiality duration, recordable traffic share, data turnover, and a fitted quantum-arrival law, with a competing-risks factor to avoid double counting. Simulations, adaptive quadrature, and an independent implementation verify the calculation, while public case studies show that long-lived, quiet, recordable assets can move sharply in priority.
main_result: The authors derive and validate an ordered cost-of-delay framework that jointly ranks classical and quantum migration risks.
application_angle: It gives security teams a practical method for deciding which communication systems or data assets should migrate to post-quantum cryptography first.

title: Heating and Escape of Confined Atoms Subject to Colored Noise
abstract: The motion of a particle in a finite-depth confining potential, such as that of an electromagnetically trapped atom or ion, is approximately harmonic at low energy and softens as the escape energy is approached. When the particle is driven by a stochastic force, the heating and escape times depend sensitively on the noise power spectrum. We study escape times of particles in softening potentials driven by power-law colored noise. We identify two nested conditions for weak noise: the particle must execute many oscillations before escape, and noise forces must be small relative to forces exerted by the trap so as not to tilt the potential appreciably. In this regime, we derive expressions for the mean escape time using stochastic averaging techniques and compare them with Monte Carlo simulations of the full equations of motion. We also examine the crossover to regimes where these conditions are not met and large quasi-static forces give rise to additional escape mechanisms. Applying these results to an experimental measurement of lifetimes in a microfabricated ion trap, we find that spectral color alone cannot account for the rapid escape rates observed, whereas quasi-static barrier tilting by a stray field of plausible magnitude could. These results are relevant to the heating and escape of trapped atoms due to noisy force fields, as well as to other nonlinear oscillators subject to colored noise.
one_liner: Models heating and escape of trapped atoms or ions in finite-depth softening potentials under power-law colored noise.
why_it_matters: Noise-driven atom loss limits trapped-ion and trapped-atom hardware, and escape rates depend strongly on realistic noise spectra and stray fields.
detailed_summary: The paper studies particles in finite-depth trapping potentials that are harmonic at low energy but soften near escape. Using stochastic averaging, it derives mean escape-time expressions for weak power-law colored noise and compares them with full Monte Carlo simulations. Applied to a microfabricated ion-trap lifetime measurement, the analysis finds that spectral color alone cannot explain rapid escape, while plausible quasi-static stray-field tilting can.
main_result: The study derives colored-noise escape-time models and identifies quasi-static barrier tilting as a plausible mechanism for observed rapid ion loss.
application_angle: It helps diagnose and mitigate trap-noise and stray-field limits in trapped-ion quantum hardware and precision sensing platforms.

title: Geometric heat pumping on a quantum processor
abstract: Geometric heat pumping is the transfer of energy between reservoirs at equal temperature where the heat exchanged in an adiabatic cycle depends only on the driving contour in parameter space. We implement this mechanism on a superconducting quantum processor using a collision model, where a driven qubit interacts repeatedly with two ancilla qubits that are prepared in thermal states and emulate the reservoirs. Energy measurements before and after each interaction provide a calorimetric record of the heat exchanged with each reservoir. By reversing the driving contour, we extract a heat contribution associated with pumping. Its dependence on the period and on the contour follows exact simulations of the collision model, without adjustable parameters, and approaches in the slow-driving regime the geometric limit of the corresponding Lindblad dynamics.
one_liner: Superconducting qubits emulate geometric heat pumping between equal-temperature reservoirs using a collision-model calorimetry protocol.
why_it_matters: It turns a thermodynamic effect usually treated theoretically into a measurable processor-level primitive for quantum heat transport and control.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses a driven superconducting qubit repeatedly coupled to two ancilla qubits prepared as effective thermal reservoirs. Energy measurements before and after each interaction build a calorimetric record of exchanged heat. Reversing the driving contour isolates the pumped heat contribution, whose period and contour dependence match exact collision-model simulations and approach the Lindblad geometric limit in slow driving.
main_result: The work demonstrates geometric heat pumping on a superconducting processor with no-adjustable-parameter agreement to collision-model simulations.
application_angle: The protocol is relevant to engineered quantum thermal machines, calorimetry, and thermodynamic benchmarking of quantum hardware.

title: Interaction-Assisted Spin Coherence in a Multimode Trapped Atomic Ensemble
abstract: In a thermally occupied multimode trapped ensemble, mode-dependent detunings can strongly suppress Ramsey contrast even when the underlying dynamics remains coherent. We develop a weak-axis-resolved Hamiltonian theory in which collective mode spins experience longitudinal detunings and overlap-dependent exchange interactions. Without exchange, the distribution of detunings across thermally occupied modes produces coherent phase mixing and an algebraically decaying Ramsey-contrast envelope in the many-mode continuum regime. At the mean-field level, exchange generates a self-consistent restoring field that reduces phase dispersion and restores collective contrast. The crossover is governed by the competition between the collective exchange scale and the thermally induced detuning spread: when the late-time contrast is expressed in terms of their ratio, results at different temperatures collapse onto a common trend, and the crossover coupling follows the predicted inverse-square thermal scaling, with a numerical exponent of 2.06. Weak irreversible pure dephasing limits, but does not eliminate, this recovery, demonstrating that exchange refocuses coherent inhomogeneous phase mixing but cannot reverse irreversible phase noise.
one_liner: Exchange interactions restore Ramsey contrast in a thermally occupied multimode trapped atomic ensemble by refocusing coherent phase mixing.
why_it_matters: Controlling inhomogeneous dephasing in multimode ensembles is central for atomic clocks, quantum memories, and precision sensors.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a weak-axis-resolved Hamiltonian model where thermally populated modes acquire different longitudinal detunings and overlap-dependent exchange couplings. Without exchange, the detuning distribution causes coherent phase mixing and algebraic Ramsey-contrast decay. Mean-field exchange produces a restoring field that suppresses phase dispersion, with crossover behavior collapsing versus the ratio of exchange scale to thermal detuning spread and following an inverse-square thermal scaling.
main_result: The main result is an interaction-assisted recovery of collective Ramsey contrast despite thermally induced multimode detunings.
application_angle: This provides a route to longer useful coherence in ensemble-based clocks, interferometers, and atom-photonic quantum interfaces.

title: Achieving a long lifetime synchronized state in a thermal vapor Rydberg time crystal
abstract: Time crystals are a unique and recently discovered state of matter in which time-translational symmetry is spontaneously broken. Although this state has been observed across a variety of quantum systems, understanding the nature between driving, dissipation, and noise and the effects of these forces on the state lifetime remains elusive. Here, we study phase diffusion and entrainment of the time crystalline oscillatory state of a thermal-vapor Rydberg atom ensemble. We apply a pulsed rf heterodyne driving field which can entrain the oscillation frequency during the on driving period. During the off period, the entrained ensemble phase diffuses on a 1/$e$ timescale up to 2.3 ms -- significantly longer than the Rydberg state lifetime. We additionally study how the entrainment and phase diffusion timescales are affected by the strength and detuning of the rf driving field, and develop a classical Fokker-Planck model with an Adler-based driving term that reproduces the observed experimental findings. These results demonstrate the creation of a long-time synchronized time crystal Rydberg atom ensemble state, which could be utilized in applications requiring frequency and phase stability.
one_liner: A thermal-vapor Rydberg ensemble shows millisecond-scale synchronized time-crystal phase memory under pulsed rf heterodyne entrainment.
why_it_matters: Long-lived phase synchronization in warm vapor Rydberg systems could support compact frequency references and phase-stable quantum devices.
detailed_summary: The study probes phase diffusion and entrainment in a thermal-vapor Rydberg time-crystalline oscillatory state. A pulsed rf heterodyne drive locks the oscillation during the on period, after which the ensemble phase diffuses with a 1/e timescale up to 2.3 ms, far exceeding the Rydberg lifetime. Drive strength and detuning dependencies are captured by a classical Fokker-Planck model with an Adler-based driving term.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates a long-lifetime synchronized Rydberg time-crystal state with phase memory up to 2.3 ms.
application_angle: The result points toward vapor-cell platforms for phase-stable oscillators, synchronization elements, and rf-sensitive quantum hardware.

title: The coupler Eve did not monitor: a black-box cavity cheat
abstract: Eve receives two average photon counts, while a monitor watching for external leakage may register nothing. Can she conclude that Alice and Bob's opaque cavity devices did not communicate? We give a constructive counterexample: two independently operated controls activate a shared beam-splitter interaction after the inputs arrive. The parties report genuine sample averages, and a fixed local threshold converts these reports into a CHSH game with expected score $S=13/4$ for four repetitions per block, approaching $4$ for large blocks in the ideal model. This exceeds the usual $2\sqrt2$ quantum benchmark because the devices interact during their response. A separate dispersive-bus model explains how substantial exchange can coexist with a small probability of a click in a specified leakage monitor; an illustrative open-system calculation exhibits both effects without postselection. The output marginals nevertheless reveal signalling. The example separates three questions: whether the reports are honest, whether a monitored port is quiet, and whether the devices are physically isolated.
one_liner: A black-box cavity model shows that quiet leakage monitoring does not prove two opaque devices were physically isolated.
why_it_matters: It highlights a concrete loophole for device-independence tests and secure quantum communication assumptions based on limited monitoring.
detailed_summary: The paper constructs a counterexample in which two independently operated controls activate a shared beam-splitter interaction after inputs arrive. The devices can report honest sample averages that exceed the usual quantum CHSH benchmark because they physically interact during response generation. A dispersive-bus model further shows that sizable exchange can coexist with low click probability in a specified leakage monitor, while output marginals reveal signalling.
platform_or_system: opaque cavity devices with shared coupler
main_result: The work demonstrates that honest reports and a quiet monitored port are insufficient to certify device isolation.
application_angle: This is directly relevant to side-channel analysis, certification assumptions, and physical-security design in quantum communication experiments.

title: Low-Cost Spectrophotometers: A Comparative Evaluation of Open-Source Architectures
abstract: The rapid growth of low-cost and open-source spectrophotometers has created a need for systematic methodologies to evaluate and compare alternative instrument architectures. This study presents a comparative assessment of three representative open-source spectrophotometric platforms, encompassing discrete multispectral sensing and continuous-spectrum imaging approaches. Their performance was evaluated against a commercial Thermo Scientific Genesys 30 spectrophotometer in terms of spectral agreement, portability, implementation complexity, and cost. The results demonstrate that no single architecture is universally optimal; instead, each presents distinct trade-offs that determine its suitability for specific applications. Multispectral sensor-based systems offer compact, low-power solutions for field deployment, whereas imaging-based platforms provide spectral performance closer to laboratory-grade instrumentation. All hardware designs, firmware, and software developed in this work are released as open-source resources to support reproducibility and further development. The study highlights the importance of matching instrument architecture to application requirements and proposes a practical framework for the evaluation and selection of low-cost spectrophotometers, facilitating the adoption of open-source analytical tools for water quality monitoring and related applications.
one_liner: Three open-source low-cost spectrophotometer architectures are benchmarked against a commercial instrument for field and lab use.
why_it_matters: It gives practical selection criteria for reproducible, affordable optical sensing hardware in water-quality and analytical monitoring.
detailed_summary: The study compares representative open-source spectrophotometers spanning discrete multispectral sensing and continuous-spectrum imaging architectures. Performance is evaluated against a Thermo Scientific Genesys 30 in spectral agreement, portability, implementation complexity, and cost. The results show architecture-dependent trade-offs: multispectral systems favor compact low-power deployment, while imaging-based systems more closely approach laboratory-grade spectral performance.
main_result: The main result is a comparative framework and open release of hardware, firmware, and software for low-cost spectrophotometer selection.
application_angle: The work supports deployable optical sensors for water-quality monitoring, education, and resource-constrained analytical measurements.

title: Full molecular dynamics simulations of a single trapped ion in a neutral bath
abstract: We present full molecular dynamics simulations that explicitly incorporate the simultaneous interactions between a trapped ion and a bath of neutral atoms. In contrast to conventional molecular dynamics treatments, this framework enables a systematic assessment of how the atomic-gas density influences both the ion's cooling dynamics and its steady-state mean kinetic energy. Our results show that the gas density measurably modifies the ion's average kinetic energy, albeit only weakly, in qualitative disagreement with predictions obtained from standard molecular dynamics simulations. In addition, the calculations indicate that short-range features of the atom-ion interaction potential become increasingly consequential as the atomic density increases. Simulations including many atoms yield higher mean kinetic energies than standard molecular dynamics, a trend we attribute to the transient formation of molecular-ion complexes. Finally, we observe that for a fixed ion, lighter atomic baths lead to a smaller final ion average kinetic energy than heavier atomic baths.
one_liner: Full molecular dynamics simulations reveal density-dependent cooling and kinetic-energy shifts for a trapped ion in a neutral gas bath.
why_it_matters: Accurate atom-ion bath modeling matters for trapped-ion cooling, hybrid quantum systems, and hardware operated near background gases.
detailed_summary: The work extends molecular dynamics simulations to include simultaneous interactions between a trapped ion and many neutral atoms. It finds that atomic-gas density weakly but measurably changes the ion steady-state kinetic energy, differing qualitatively from standard molecular dynamics predictions. Higher densities make short-range atom-ion potential features more important, and many-atom simulations produce higher mean kinetic energies attributed to transient molecular-ion complex formation.
platform_or_system: single trapped ion in neutral atom bath
main_result: The simulations show that many-body bath effects and gas density alter trapped-ion cooling dynamics and final kinetic energy.
application_angle: The findings inform cooling limits and error budgets for trapped-ion processors, sensors, and hybrid atom-ion platforms.

title: Cross-Validation of Open-Source Quantum Network Simulators
abstract: We present a comparative analysis of two open-source quantum network simulators, QuISP and SeQUeNCe, focusing on cross-validation of basic networking tasks to ensure consistency and accuracy in simulation outputs. Although both simulators are designed to study quantum network management policies and their dynamics under complex noise models, their differing underlying assumptions can lead to variations in simulation results. We highlight the discrepancies in how the two simulators handle connections, internal network node processing time, and classical communication, resulting in significant quantitative and qualitative differences in the time required to perform basic network tasks such as entanglement generation, purification, and swapping. We simulate common scenarios between the simulators to compare both the latency of resource distribution and the fidelity of the distributed resources. Our findings indicate that while the simulators differ in the time required to complete network tasks---a constant factor difference attributable to their respective connection models---they agree on the fidelity of the distributed resources under identical error parameters. This work demonstrates a crucial first step towards enhancing the reliability and reproducibility of quantum network simulations, as well as leading to full protocol development. Furthermore, our benchmarking methodology establishes a foundational set of tasks for the cross-validation of simulators to study future quantum networks.
one_liner: Benchmarks QuISP and SeQUeNCe on core quantum-network tasks to expose simulator-dependent latency differences.
why_it_matters: Reliable quantum-network design needs reproducible simulators; this work separates timing-model discrepancies from agreement on delivered-state fidelity.
detailed_summary: The paper compares two open-source quantum-network simulators on shared scenarios for entanglement generation, purification, and swapping. It finds substantial quantitative and qualitative differences in task completion time, mainly from connection models, node processing time, and classical communication treatment. Under identical error parameters, the simulators agree on the fidelity of distributed resources, suggesting timing models are the main divergence.
main_result: QuISP and SeQUeNCe show constant-factor latency differences for basic tasks while matching distributed-resource fidelity under common error settings.
application_angle: The benchmark suite supports more trustworthy protocol development and planning for future quantum-network deployments.

title: Building codes with transversal CCZ using projective geometry and SAT solvers
abstract: We construct CSS codes with three logical qubits whose logical CCZ gate is implemented by transversal physical $T/T^{\dagger}$ gates and whose distance is at least $3$. These codes start with $8$-divisible $X$-stabilizers defined by projective geometry, which guarantees $d_Z\geq 3$. A SAT solver then finds three $X$-logical operators compatible with the transversal CCZ. We build codes at thirteen block lengths from $n=48$ to $n=496$, with $d_Z=3$ or $4$, and illustrate the method with the $[[48,3,3]]$ code $Q_{48}$. Additionally, we prove that no CSS code with three logical qubits, $Z$-distance at least $3$, and a quasi-transversal CCZ gate (transversal $T$ with a diagonal Clifford correction) exists below $n=39$. The $[[47,3,3]]$ code of Jacinto et al. serves as an upper bound, leaving $39\leq n\leq46$ open.
one_liner: Constructs CSS codes enabling logical CCZ via transversal physical T/T-dagger gates using projective geometry plus SAT search.
why_it_matters: Transversal non-Clifford gates are valuable for fault-tolerant quantum computing because they can reduce overhead for universal logic.
detailed_summary: The authors build CSS codes with three logical qubits where logical CCZ is realized by transversal physical T or T-dagger gates. Projective-geometry-derived 8-divisible X stabilizers ensure Z-distance at least 3, while a SAT solver identifies compatible X logical operators. They report thirteen code lengths from n=48 to n=496 and analyze the [[48,3,3]] example, while proving a nonexistence result below n=39 for a quasi-transversal variant.
main_result: The work constructs multiple distance-3-or-4 CSS codes supporting transversal CCZ and proves no qualifying quasi-transversal code exists below n=39.
application_angle: Such codes could lower resource costs for non-Clifford operations in fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Non-Orthogonal Amplitude Amplification for Hybrid CV-DV Quantum Processors
abstract: We introduce a non-orthogonal amplitude amplification (NOAA) method for hybrid continuous-variable- discrete-variable (CV-DV) quantum processors, where the available CV-assisted projector is not perfectly se- lective for the target state. We establish a bound on the achievable target-state fidelity, which is determined by the initial target-state amplitude and the selectivity of the accessible reflection operator. This bound limits the performance of NOAA in hybrid CV-DV systems. To mitigate this limitation, we propose using a squeezed CV ancilla to reduce the overlap between relevant CV states and a hybrid quantum signal processing (HQSP) filter to suppress errors arising from imperfect knowledge of the target eigenenergy. Numerical simulations show that, for small initial target-state amplitudes, our protocol achieves higher fidelity and efficiency than the repeat-until-success (RUS) method despite the presence of non-orthogonality. For large initial amplitudes, RUS is already efficient, and amplitude amplification provides little additional advantage.
one_liner: Proposes non-orthogonal amplitude amplification for hybrid CV-DV processors with imperfect target-state selectivity.
why_it_matters: Hybrid CV-DV architectures need algorithms that tolerate realistic, nonideal projectors while preserving useful fidelity and efficiency.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces NOAA, an amplitude-amplification protocol for hybrid continuous-variable and discrete-variable processors when the available CV-assisted reflection is not perfectly selective. It derives a fidelity bound set by initial target amplitude and reflection selectivity, then proposes squeezed CV ancillae and hybrid quantum signal processing filters to mitigate overlap and eigenenergy errors. Simulations show improved fidelity and efficiency over repeat-until-success for small initial target amplitudes.
main_result: NOAA can outperform repeat-until-success in simulated small-amplitude regimes despite non-orthogonal CV-assisted projections.
application_angle: The method targets more practical algorithmic primitives for hardware where CV controls and measurements are inherently imperfect.

title: Electromagnetically Transmissive and Thermally Opaque Engineered Microwave Interconnect
abstract: In a standard two-conductor microwave transmission line, both the signal trace and the wide ground plane act as parasitic heat leakage paths along the propagation direction. To prevent this heat leakage, we devised a single-conductor microwave interconnect: the ground plane is removed entirely and the remaining signal trace is periodically fragmented into physically isolated metallic islands. We show that despite the galvanic isolation between adjacent metal islands, a surface confined mode of specific symmetry, the odd-symmetric spoof surface plasmon polariton, propagates through this periodic, single-conductor medium. This odd symmetry imposes an electromagnetic field null at the waveguide centerline, allowing complete removal of the metal at periodic intervals along the single-conductor waveguide without impacting EM propagation. Measurements on fabricated prototypes confirm the transmission response despite the physical fragmentation of the conductor, with de-embedded propagation loss of ~0.0031 dB/mm across a 5-6.5 GHz passband. Time-domain characterization verifies 1 Gbps amplitude-modulated data transmission with less than 145 ps group delay variation. Coupled electro-thermal simulation yields an effective thermal conductivity of 0.336 W/m*K, a 40x reduction relative to a continuous microstrip line of identical footprint.
one_liner: Demonstrates a fragmented single-conductor microwave interconnect that transmits 5-6.5 GHz signals while suppressing heat flow.
why_it_matters: Cryogenic and quantum hardware need microwave wiring with low thermal conductance, and this design attacks heat leakage without sacrificing data transmission.
detailed_summary: The authors remove the ground plane and fragment the remaining signal conductor into isolated metallic islands, relying on an odd-symmetric spoof surface plasmon polariton mode for propagation. Fabricated prototypes show de-embedded propagation loss of about 0.0031 dB/mm across a 5-6.5 GHz passband. Time-domain tests demonstrate 1 Gbps amplitude-modulated transmission with under 145 ps group-delay variation, while simulations indicate a 40x thermal-conductivity reduction versus a continuous microstrip.
main_result: A physically fragmented single-conductor line transmits microwave data with low loss and achieves an effective thermal conductivity of 0.336 W/m*K.
application_angle: This could improve cryogenic wiring for quantum processors by reducing heat load from room-temperature control lines.

title: Compact Fully Integrated Alignment-Free and Linearly Polarized Ho$^{3+}$ Single-Frequency Waveguide Laser
abstract: We report, for the first time, a fully integrated Ho$^{3+}$-doped fluoride glass waveguide laser incorporating a femtosecond laser-inscribed waveguide and waveguide Bragg grating. The compact 12.4 mm cavity achieves stable single-frequency lasing at 2062.21 nm with a line width of better than 5 MHz. The laser emits linearly polarized light, which is efficiently delivered through an SM1950 single-mode fiber. This alignment-free architecture provides a compact and robust platform for integrated mid-infrared single-frequency laser sources.
one_liner: Reports a 12.4 mm fully integrated Ho-doped fluoride-glass waveguide laser emitting single-frequency 2062.21 nm light.
why_it_matters: Compact alignment-free mid-infrared single-frequency sources are useful for sensing, spectroscopy, and integrated photonic systems.
detailed_summary: The work presents a fully integrated Ho3+-doped fluoride-glass waveguide laser combining a femtosecond-laser-inscribed waveguide with a waveguide Bragg grating. The 12.4 mm cavity produces stable single-frequency lasing at 2062.21 nm with linewidth better than 5 MHz. The output is linearly polarized and coupled through SM1950 single-mode fiber, giving an alignment-free integrated source architecture.
main_result: The device achieves stable linearly polarized single-frequency lasing at 2062.21 nm from a compact fully integrated cavity.
application_angle: The architecture is promising for robust deployable mid-infrared spectroscopy and sensing light sources.

title: Using Learning Analytics to Study Novice Learners' Work on Quantum Circuit Simulator Tasks
abstract: Interactive quantum circuit simulators are increasingly used to support introductory quantum computing education for learners from varied disciplinary backgrounds. These environments can also generate detailed response logs of submitted circuits, but such data are rarely transformed into evidence that instructors can use for course redesign and development. We present a learning analytics framework for quantum circuit simulator tasks and report its task-level branch on anonymised logs from an introductory quantum computing course delivered in the TIM learning environment. The task branch characterises exercises through participation, completion, first-attempt accuracy, valid-attempt counts, sessionised active time, and observed answer-space reporting of common correct and incorrect constructions. The dataset covers the 2024-2025 cohort of 492 learners, 47,533 valid submissions, and 21 obligatory quantum circuit exercises. The framework identifies bottleneck tasks, broad solution spaces, and recurring wrong-answer patterns that are not visible from final scores alone. Its most distinctive output is a plain-text representation of the observed answer space, designed to make open-ended circuit submissions directly interpretable to instructors. We show how response logs can reveal actionable task-design issues and support concrete course redesign. A learner-level branch is retained only as an ongoing research extension and is not a central empirical contribution of the present paper.
one_liner: Uses learning analytics on quantum-circuit simulator logs to reveal task bottlenecks and common wrong circuit constructions.
why_it_matters: Quantum education platforms can turn raw simulator submissions into actionable evidence for improving course and task design.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes anonymized quantum-circuit simulator logs from a 2024-2025 introductory course with 492 learners and 47,533 valid submissions across 21 obligatory exercises.
