one_liner: Gives a polylog-depth circuit block-encoding generator-representable semiseparable matrices from their generators.
why_it_matters: It supplies an efficient primitive for quantum algorithms using structured numerical matrices.

title: Percolation of Data Constraints and Reorganization of Boolean Function States in Parity Learning
abstract: We study how a neural network reorganizes its learned function as training proceeds and as previously unseen parity data accumulate. The trained model is itself a Boolean function on binary strings of finite length. We then evaluate it on all data, inside and outside the training set, and read off its complete sign table. Its $\pm1$ entries are the amplitudes of a normalized state, dubbed the function-state, whose inverse subsystem purity $K_f=1/\textrm{Tr}(ρ_A^2)$ is an effective Schmidt rank. We find that small data additions broaden the Schmidt spectrum, whereas larger additions reconcentrate it in the target mode. The former is called differentiation because the model distinguishes inputs more sharply. The latter is called target-selective recoherence, where the model settles on the single rule shared by the added data. As the dataset grows, the connectivity of the constraint graph defined by the training set increases monotonically, whereas the learned inverse purity changes nonmonotonically. On a fixed connected dataset, as learning proceeds, the Schmidt spectrum begins to reorganize, followed by gains in target alignment and later by improvement in predictive accuracy. This ordering distinguishes three aspects of learning: constraint identifiability, function-state organization, and predictive accuracy. At fixed data size, a function that has already been learned can re-differentiate, an event we call retreat, without changing graph connectivity. Recovery reconcentrates the Schmidt spectrum in a similar target-selective pattern, without exact recurrence of the Boolean state. Thus the percolation of data constraints fixes the identifiable support, while the reduced state produced by training continues to reorganize even after that support stops changing.
one_liner: Studies parity-learning networks via Boolean function-states, linking data-constraint percolation to nonmonotonic Schmidt-spectrum reorganization.
why_it_matters: It separates identifiability, internal function organization, and predictive accuracy in a compact learning model.

title: Theory of exciton-exciton interactions in crystalline systems
abstract: Excitons are bound electron-hole pairs in semiconductors whose interactions influence optical properties and determine their collective behavior and emergent correlated phases. Despite the theoretical and experimental significance of these phenomena, a microscopic theory of exciton-exciton interactions that takes into account the full composite nature of these quasiparticles is lacking. Here, we present a general theory of exciton-exciton interactions that builds upon our previous publication [Physical Review B 113, 155440 (2026)], which applied only to conventional semiconductors with weak band hybridization. By contrast, the theory presented here is valid in virtually any crystalline semiconducting system and can be applied to the study of biexciton formation and correlated excitonic phases in systems where band topology, quantum geometry, and moiré effects play a significant role. In addition to the analytical theory, we also present results in simple systems with flat bands with a nontrivial quantum metric and show that the biexcitonic spectrum differs strongly from that in the case without quantum geometry. Our theory paves the way for accurate quantitative calculations of biexciton spectra and excitonic many-body phases in modern condensed-matter systems.
one_liner: Develops a general microscopic theory of exciton-exciton interactions for crystalline semiconductors beyond weak band hybridization.
why_it_matters: It enables quantitative treatment of biexcitons and correlated excitonic phases in topological, geometric, and moire systems.

title: Zak Phase Quantization without Global Symmetry through Destructive Interference
abstract: The Zak phase provides a fundamental geometric characterization of one-dimensional band structures and, when quantized by symmetry, serves as a bulk indicator of polarization and boundary phenomena. Conventionally, its exact quantization is tied to a global symmetry of the Bloch Hamiltonian, such as inversion or reflection symmetry. Here, we demonstrate a distinct mechanism by which the Zak phase remains exactly quantized even when the corresponding protecting symmetry is explicitly broken at the level of the full Hamiltonian. The mechanism is based on local support symmetry and destructive interference: symmetry-breaking degrees of freedom are coupled to a topological parent system in such a way that the relevant Bloch states cannot leak into them. The preserved states therefore retain their parent wave functions and inherit their quantized Zak phase exactly, despite the absence of the protecting global symmetry. We establish this mechanism for general one-dimensional insulators and demonstrate it in an inversion-broken minimal model and a reflection-broken armchair nanoribbon, where a quantized $π$ Zak phase and associated boundary-localized states persist. We further show that perturbations violating the exact destructive-interference condition continuously dequantize the Zak phase, while a finite regime with a near-$π$ Zak phase and boundary response can survive. Our results establish wave-function support, rather than global symmetry alone, as a mechanism for protecting quantized quantum geometry in one-dimensional systems.
one_liner: Shows exact Zak-phase quantization can persist without global symmetry through local support symmetry and destructive interference.
why_it_matters: It broadens how protected quantum geometry and boundary states can arise in one-dimensional systems.

title: Solitons in the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with the pseudo-Raman term, anti-diffusion gain and nonlinear loss
abstract: We introduce a nonconservative nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) which includes additional nonlinear terms accounting for the pseudo-stimulated-Raman-scattering (pseudo-SRS) effect and cubic loss. An essentially novel feature of the model is the linear anti-diffusion gain, which leads to the obvious blow-up in the infinite or spatially periodic system. We consider the absorptive boundary conditions, which suppress the blow-up driven by effective convective instability in the setup. The NSLE model is derived, in the extended adiabatic approximation, from the underlying Zakharov system, which includes the viscosity term acting on its low-frequency component and the anti-diffusion gain in the high-frequency (HF) one. The latter term appears if the expansion, with respect to the deviation of the wavenumber, is performed not around the minimum-loss point (as in the usual situation), but around a maximum-loss point. Dynamics of moving solitons in the model is addressed by means of analytical and numerical methods. The sech approximation for the soliton predicts it as a stable fixed point (FP) of the system of balance equations for the HF norm and wave momentum, derived in the moving reference frame. The FP attraction basin is identified too. The predictions are corroborated by direct simulations of the full NSLE with the absorptive boundary conditions.
one_liner: Analyzes moving solitons in a nonconservative NLSE with pseudo-Raman terms, anti-diffusion gain, nonlinear loss, and absorptive boundaries.
why_it_matters: It identifies stability conditions for solitons in gain-driven systems that would otherwise blow up.

title: Circuit Design Problems in Binary Polynomial Quantum Optimization
abstract: Solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum computers mainly relies on their quadratic unconstrained binary formulation. Lately, binary polynomial formulations start to take the center stage, having a better scaling with respect to the number of used qubits. However, while quadratic forms are straightforward to implement on quantum circuits, polynomial forms of degree $d$ incur in circuit depth overheads, due to the lack of $d$-qubit gates, for $d\geq 3$, on current hardware. In this paper, we study the problem of designing the shallowest quantum circuit for a given polynomial form. We formulate it as a classical binary linear problem and we prove the \textsf{NP}-completeness of a variant of it. On the algorithmic side, we offer a scalable and performant heuristic method to tackle it, Tempura, as well as faster binary linear problem formulations, which offer computational feasibility while sacrificing optimality. Our performance evaluation shows that the algorithms yield far shorter circuits than the state-of-the-art approaches, and Tempura is mostly comparable with them in terms of runtime.
one_liner: Formulates shallow circuit design for binary polynomial quantum optimization and introduces the Tempura heuristic.
why_it_matters: Shorter circuits can make higher-degree polynomial encodings more practical on near-term quantum hardware.

title: Recovering Irreducible Three-Body Interactions with Lagrangian Neural Networks
abstract: Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) learn mechanical systems from trajectory data by parameterizing a scalar Lagrangian and deriving the dynamics through the Euler-Lagrange equations, biasing the model toward motion that respects the variational structure of mechanics. The interactions studied so far have been pairwise-additive, leaving open whether LNNs can recover an irreducible many-body interaction from motion alone. We address this using the Axilrod-Teller triple-dipole interaction, the leading three-body dispersion term, whose dependence on the collective geometry of three particles cannot be represented by any sum of pairwise terms. We prescribe the kinetic energy exactly and learn only the potential, as a function of interparticle distances and angles. Combined with a signal-aware sampling strategy that concentrates training data where the three-body signal is strongest while preserving broad coverage of configuration space, this recovers the interaction from accelerations alone. The learned potential reproduces the radial scaling, angular dependence, and characteristic sign reversal of the Axilrod-Teller interaction, and generates stable trajectories. Embedding it within a pairwise Lennard-Jones potential lets us examine its observability: the three-body term is recovered once its dynamical signature exceeds the residual modeling error, which it does cleanly at amplified coupling but not at the coupling of a real noble gas, bracketing the transition between the two. Finally, symbolic regression on the trained potential, with no assumed functional form, returns the Axilrod-Teller expression with angular numerator, radial law, and coupling constant intact. An LNN with domain-specific structure can thus recover an irreducible three-body interaction from trajectories as a closed-form law, pointing toward learning interaction laws whose structure is not known a priori.
one_liner: Uses Lagrangian neural networks to recover the irreducible Axilrod-Teller three-body interaction from trajectory data.
why_it_matters: It shows structured learning can infer non-pairwise physical laws and recover them symbolically from dynamics.

title: A General Method for Extending Isoscattering Non-Isospectral Quantum Graphs
abstract: The present paper sets out a general method for extending the isoscattering, non-isospectral quantum graphs. The methodology is illustrated by considering two graphs, denoted by $Γ_1$ and $Γ_2$, which have the same total metric length but different topologies. It is demonstrated that, despite the fact that their scattering matrices are identical, their eigenvalues, denoted by $k_n$, and Euler characteristics differ from one another. The next step in the process is to extend both graphs by affixing the same star graph to each of them. Utilising the Titchmarsh-Weyl M-function formalism, it is proven that the newly constructed, extended graphs are also isoscattering and non-isospectral.
one_liner: Presents a method for extending quantum graphs while preserving isoscattering behavior despite non-isospectral structure.
why_it_matters: It clarifies how scattering equivalence can survive graph extensions even when spectra and topology differ.

title: Second quantization and compactness of induced Gaussian quantum Markov semigroups
abstract: We characterize compactness of the Hilbert-Schmidt semigroups induced by finite-mode Gaussian quantum Markov semigroups with a faithful normal invariant state. A unitary second-quantization representation for every $ s $-embedding shows that compactness at one positive time, compact resolvent, drift stability, and uniqueness of the normal invariant state are equivalent. These conditions imply immediate trace-class membership for all embeddings. We derive exact trace-norm and Hilbert--Schmidt norm formulas, an embedding-independent trace identity, and the generator spectrum with algebraic multiplicities. Examples show that compactness does not require the existence of a spectral gap and that a spectral gap need not imply compactness when the invariant state is not unique.
one_liner: Characterizes compactness and spectra of Hilbert-Schmidt semigroups induced by finite-mode Gaussian quantum Markov semigroups.
why_it_matters: It connects compactness, invariant-state uniqueness, drift stability, and resolvent structure in Gaussian open systems.

title: Bottom-Up Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering for the Detection of Micro-Objects and Globular Analytes
abstract: Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) is typically achieved by depositing the analyte on a metal or semiconductor substrate. We propose a bottom-up approach, enabling SERS by depositing a metal on the surface of the object being studied. A Mie-theory analysis of electric-field enhancement in dielectric core-shell particles is presented. A correlative approach combining SERS, atomic force microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy is employed to model the conditions required for sensitive SERS detection and spectral analysis of polystyrene microspheres (PMSs) as models of globular and vesicle-like objects. Based on these findings, we propose a SERS-active system that provides strong signal enhancement (up to four orders of magnitude for a single globular object) while maintaining spectral fidelity, where PMSs act both as model analytes and as integral components of a metal-dielectric resonator.
one_liner: Proposes bottom-up SERS by depositing metal onto globular analytes and models dielectric core-shell enhancement.
why_it_matters: It offers a route to sensitive Raman analysis of micro-objects while preserving spectral fidelity.

title: Quantum extreme learning for forecasting experimental chaotic electronic circuits
abstract: Quantum reservoir computing and its special case, quantum extreme learning, are powerful tools for predicting classical discrete time-series with quantum devices. Forecasting continuous signals, however, requires careful discretization as oversampling artificially boosts short-term accuracy but fails over realistic intervals, while undersampling captures too few features and yields poor predictions. Here, we experimentally generate four continuous time-series signals from a chaotic electronic circuit for forecasting with quantum extreme learning. Since simplified circuit models do not fully capture real behaviour, it is unclear whether algorithms that predict simulated time-series also work for experimental signals. We address discretization via two approaches: (i) sampling local peaks/troughs; and (ii) uniform sampling at the autocorrelation timescale. The former captures resonant behaviour, while the latter fully captures chaotic features as well as allowing the reconstruction of chaotic attractors. Our algorithm achieves high forecasting accuracy for both simulated and experimental signals, demonstrating its power for continuous signal processing on near-term quantum simulators, and remains robust against moderate decoherence.
one_liner: Demonstrates quantum extreme learning for forecasting continuous chaotic signals from experimental electronic circuits.
why_it_matters: It tests quantum forecasting on real chaotic data and highlights sampling choices that avoid misleading accuracy.

title: Localization Landscapes based on the Green's Matrix of Non-Hermitian Optical Scattering Systems
abstract: The Filoche--Mayboroda (FM) localization landscape predicts where the spatially localized modes of a self-adjoint elliptic operator reside without diagonalizing it, but the construction fails for the complex, non-normal Green's matrix G of an open scattering array of electric dipoles. We propose three real-valued, positive landscapes built from the Feinberg--Zee hermitization of G: a regularised Gramian inverse (Gram), the diagonal Schur block that carries the Metz--Neri--Rogers spectral density (SY), and the full hermitized inverse contracted against a polarization-isotropic source pair (Herm). The three form a progression from spectrum-blind to fully hermitisation-faithful, agree in the limit $z\to 0$, and diverge where it matters: at nonzero spectral shift SY resolves modes that Gram collapses, and Herm resolves modes that SY collapses. We demonstrate the progression on random and deterministic aperiodic scattering arrays with a wide range of structural correlations, extend to the vectorial case of transverse electric polarization (TE), and provide rigorous justifications along with mathematical proofs and a complete numerical recipe in the appendices and in the supplementary material.
one_liner: Introduces positive localization landscapes for non-Hermitian optical scattering Green matrices via Feinberg-Zee hermitization.
why_it_matters: It provides practical mode-localization predictors for complex open scattering arrays without full diagonalization.

title: Spectral-control-assisted Kerr-lens mode-locking in a Tm:Y2O3 ceramic laser
abstract: We report a soft-aperture Kerr-lens mode-locked Tm:Y2O3 ceramic laser stabilized by suppressing wavelength competition under high population-inversion conditions. The laser delivers an average output power of 0.5 W with a pulse duration of 112 fs at a repetition rate of 90 MHz and a central wavelength of 2.08 um. Further optimization for shorter pulses yields a pulse duration of 107 fs, through with a reduced output power of 0.22 W. These results demonstrate that spectral-control is an effective approach for achieving stable mode-locking in such laser with strong spectral competition.
one_liner: Reports spectral-control-assisted Kerr-lens mode-locking in a Tm:Y2O3 ceramic laser producing sub-120 fs pulses near 2.08 um.
why_it_matters: It shows spectral control can stabilize mode-locking under strong wavelength competition in Tm ceramic lasers.

title: Finite Quantum Engineering Thermodynamics
abstract: A useful thermodynamic model predicts what a device will do without tracking its full microscopic state. For a finite quantum working medium, the difficult question is which quantities should actually be measured. We develop a task-based method that keeps exact energy accounting separate from calibrated macroscopic prediction. Operator geometry identifies what a measured record determines and bounds what remains uncertain. We then compare direct measurements of dynamical observables with earlier measurements of the same coarse record, selecting the representation together with its measurement cost. A Bose--Hubbard example yields a compact response table tested over a continuous operating region and on unseen microscopic trajectories. A driven Ising chain shows why history is not always the cheaper choice. The result is a way to turn detailed quantum dynamics into a small, reusable, and explicitly qualified thermodynamic description.
one_liner: A task-based framework compresses finite quantum dynamics into reusable thermodynamic response descriptions with explicit uncertainty bounds.
why_it_matters: It clarifies what must be measured to make finite quantum devices predictable without tracking every microscopic detail.

title: Construction of isoscattering non-isospectral quantum graphs using the concept of a germ graph
abstract: The recently developed concept of germ graphs (P. Kurasov {\it et al.}, Phys. Rev. Research {\bf 7}, L022071 (2025)) is employed to construct families of isocattering, non-isospectral graphs that exhibit dissipation. More specifically, a new pair of isoscattering non-isospectral graphs is constructed by connecting the existing isoscattering non-isospectral graphs, so called attachments, to the different contact vertices of the germ graph. The existing isoscattering non-isospectral graphs contained a two-loop graph labelled $Γ_{A2}$ and a three-loop graph labelled $Γ_{A3}$. These graphs have an equal total metric length, but different topologies. The resulting graphs $Γ_3$ and $Γ_4$ are verified as non-isospectral using their Euler characteristics, while their isoscattering properties are investigated by calculating the one-port scattering matrices numerically.
one_liner: Germ graphs are used to build dissipative quantum graph pairs that share scattering behavior but differ in spectra and topology.
why_it_matters: It expands constructive tools for studying spectral versus scattering information in open quantum graph systems.

title: UV Fluorescence Sensing of Medical-Chemical-and- Biological Analytes by an AlGaN/Si-on-Sapphire Optoelectronic Chip
abstract: This paper proposes and analyzes a compact fluorescence-photometer lab-on-a-chip that is simpler than a fluorescence spectrometer, and that does not require spectrum reconstruction by a computer. An on-chip AlGaN VCSEL lasing at 280 nm, or at 310 nm, pumps an on-chip sample in the form of liquid or solid or tissue, thereby exciting signature fluorescence in the 300 to 540 nm wavelength range. This emission signal is detected and read out by an on-chip UV-enhanced Silicon photodiode. The 2 cm x 5 cm chip consists of C-plane (0001) Sapphire, and no lenses, prisms, or mirrors are utilized in the photometer. The chip is opto-electronic and features co-packaged electronics using tiny electronic chiplets that are bonded to the sapphire. These consist of an LD driver and transimpedance amplifier for the UV photonics, together with ASICs, ADC, microcontroller, micro-battery and RF-wireless or Ethernet chiplets. The mission of this self-contained cost-effective chip is sensing targeted medical-chemical-biological (MCB) agents in a local or network setting. Eight significant MCB applications are detailed here.
one_liner: A compact AlGaN/Si-on-sapphire chip is proposed for UV fluorescence sensing of medical, chemical, and biological analytes.
why_it_matters: It points toward simpler networkable fluorescence photometers without spectrometers or free-space optics.

title: Aubry-André transition in photonic time quasicrystals
abstract: In one dimension, Anderson localization by a disordered potential sets in at any strength, whereas localization by a quasiperiodic potential in the Aubry-André model occurs through a transition at a critical strength. Disordered photonic time crystals exhibit a temporal counterpart of this Anderson localization, in which light, instead of decaying in space, stops propagating and grows in time. Whether a counterpart of the Aubry-André transition exists in photonic time quasicrystals remains an open question. Here we show that it does, and that the transition occurs at mobility edges in momentum rather than in energy. These edges arise even under impulsive modulation, where the field obeys the self-dual almost-Mathieu equation exactly, and for general analytic modulations Avila's global theory reveals the condition under which they form. The Aubry-André transition thus extends from spatial lattices to the time domain, where it sorts light by wave number into components that propagate and components that stop and grow.
one_liner: The Aubry-André localization transition is shown to have a temporal analogue in photonic time quasicrystals with momentum mobility edges.
why_it_matters: It connects quasiperiodic localization physics to time-modulated photonic media and wave-number-selective light growth.

title: Holographic Krylov complexity in confining backgrounds: particle, string, and frames
abstract: We investigate holographic Krylov complexity in bottom-up holographic QCD models describing the confined phase, using the recently proposed correspondence between the growth rate of Krylov complexity and the proper radial momentum of probes, such as particles and strings, falling in the bulk spacetime. As representative confining backgrounds, we consider two horizonless geometries, namely the dilaton-deformed AdS-soliton and the deformed thermal-AdS spacetime, both arising as solutions of an Einstein-dilaton gravity system. We find that the Krylov complexity associated with a massive particle exhibits qualitatively distinct behavior in these two backgrounds when analyzed in the Einstein frame. In the deformed AdS-soliton geometry, the complexity undergoes periodic oscillations, with both the oscillation period and amplitude depending on the parameters of the model. In contrast, in the deformed thermal-AdS geometry, the complexity grows exponentially at late times and does not display oscillatory behavior. We then investigate string dynamics in the string frame and find that the Krylov complexity exhibits oscillatory behavior in both confining backgrounds. This behavior is traced to the emergence of an additional turning point in the deep infrared of the string-frame geometry. Motivated by this observation, we further analyze massive-particle dynamics in the string frame, where we find qualitatively similar behavior in the two confining backgrounds. Our results demonstrate that the Krylov complexity of confined holographic systems depends sensitively on the choice of probe and frame, while also revealing a closer correspondence between the two confining geometries in the string-frame description.
one_liner: Holographic Krylov complexity in confining QCD-like backgrounds is shown to depend strongly on probe choice and frame.
why_it_matters: It sharpens how complexity diagnostics should be interpreted in bottom-up holographic models of confinement.

title: Genuine multipartite nonlocality detection in graph states
abstract: Experimental detection of multipartite Bell nonlocality faces many challenges. The increase in the size of the system demands a higher fidelity of state preparation, a higher detection efficiency, and a larger number of correlators that need to be estimated. These issues are even more pronounced if one wishes to detect a more restrictive variant of Bell nonlocality called genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL). In this work, we introduce two classes of multipartite Bell inequalities that are capable of detecting GMNL correlations and address different experimental hurdles in GMNL detection. The first class consists of the number of correlators that scales linearly with the number of parties. The second class increases the number of correlators and, in return, provides higher noise robustness of GMNL detection. Both classes of inequalities are constructed to detect GMNL in graph states, and in fact both can be used for self-testing of graph states and the performed measurements.
one_liner: Two Bell-inequality families are introduced to detect genuine multipartite nonlocality in graph states under different resource tradeoffs.
why_it_matters: It offers more practical routes to verify strong nonlocal correlations in larger multipartite experiments.

title: Encoding Matters: A Qubit-Efficient Reformulation for Quantum Resilient Routing
abstract: Qubits are powerful computational resources because each additional qubit doubles the size of the accessible state space. This expressive power comes at a cost: adding qubits also increases circuit size, constraint overhead, and exposure to hardware noise. These limitations are especially critical for near-term quantum computers, making the number of qubits required to formulate a problem a central practical concern. In this work, we present a method for efficiently mapping logistics and routing problems onto qubits through structure-aware encoding reduction. We demonstrate the method on a benchmark problem of latency-resilient routing under dual-link failures. For this benchmark, the reduced formulation substantially lowers both the qubit count and the compiled circuit complexity while preserving the original optimization task. By running the reduced model on the same trapped-ion quantum computer as the benchmark, we obtain a 100X improvement in the success probability. This finding shows how careful problem formulation can make current quantum hardware substantially more effective for practical optimization.
one_liner: A structure-aware encoding reformulates quantum resilient routing to reduce qubits and circuit complexity while preserving the task.
why_it_matters: It shows that better encodings can greatly improve near-term quantum optimization performance on real hardware.

title: Operational signatures of exceptional quantum channels
abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) are usually introduced as defective degeneracies of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians and, in fully open quantum dynamics, of Liouvillian generators. Here we formulate an operational theory of exceptional points that does not invoke a Hamiltonian or a master equation. The primitive dynamical object is a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) quantum channel $Φ$, applied an integer number $n$ of times, while physical data are probabilities $p_n^{\mathbf A}(x|ρ)$ associated with states $ρ$ and observables $\mathbf A$ having measurements results $x$. We define exceptional channels through nontrivial Jordan chains of $Φ$ and show that a Jordan block of order $m$ generates discrete polynomial-exponential terms with maximal degree $m-1$. This places the physics of exceptional points in contact with what can be directly measured in experiments.
one_liner: Exceptional points are reformulated operationally for CPTP quantum channels using observable probability sequences and Jordan structure.
why_it_matters: It ties exceptional-channel behavior directly to measurable data without assuming a Hamiltonian or master equation.

title: Finite-Size Limits of Adaptive Pauli Prediction
abstract: Can quantum data reliably answer questions chosen from earlier results? We prove that $M$ adaptive Pauli predictions on $n$ qubits require $Ω(\sqrt{\min\{n,M\}})$ copies at fixed accuracy. Published upper bounds make this tight for $M\le n$. Thus $n$ adaptive predictions cost $Θ(\sqrt n)$ copies, whereas a fixed list costs only $O(\log n)$. The lower bound uses diagonal states and commuting observables, identifying a statistical cost of adaptation. We also quantify how this cost increases with precision.
one_liner: Adaptive Pauli prediction is proven to require square-root copy complexity, sharply separating adaptive from fixed-query regimes.
why_it_matters: It quantifies a fundamental statistical cost of asking quantum-data questions chosen from earlier answers.

title: Dynamical Lie Algebras for Fixed-Gate Quantum Ansätze
abstract: Parameterized Quantum Circuits have emerged as a central framework for variational quantum algorithms in the NISQ regime, with major applications in quantum simulation, combinatorial optimization, and, more recently, quantum machine learning (QML). By developing a new approach for computing dynamical Lie algebras associated with quantum circuits combining parametrized gates and non-parametrized entangling gates, we aim to extend the applicability of recent algebraic results to architectures that are actually used in quantum machine learning.
one_liner: A method is developed to compute dynamical Lie algebras for ansätze combining parametrized gates with fixed entangling gates.
why_it_matters: It extends algebraic expressivity analysis toward circuit architectures commonly used in quantum machine learning.

title: Chiroptical Nonlinearity Found in Covalent Organic Frameworks
abstract: Chiroptical nonlinearity is vital for modern optics and photonics. However, it remains a central challenge to obtain a material simultaneously with large second-order nonlinearity and strong nonlinear optical chirality. Here we uncover the strong chiroptical nonlinearity in COF-330-a, owing to the formation of unique chiral, polar structure with large p-electron conjugation via structural transformation. A large effective second-order nonlinear susceptibility of ~ 101 pm/V and a strong nonlinear chiroptical response (SHG-CD: -1.60 to +1.66) have been demonstrated in individual COF-330-a microcrystals, transcending the performance trade-off limitation in conventional chiroptical materials. These findings open a new avenue for designing nonlinear chiroptical crystals which harness the duality of polarity and chirality and chemical versatility of COFs.
one_liner: COF-330-a microcrystals are reported to combine strong second-order nonlinearity with large nonlinear chiroptical response.
why_it_matters: It suggests covalent organic frameworks as tunable platforms for high-performance nonlinear chiroptical photonics.

title: PhySeqNet: physics-informed fluorescent foci detection for BARseq spatial transcriptomics
abstract: BARseq enables spatially resolved gene-expression profiling across intact tissue, but its sensitivity depends on accurate detection and decoding of dense fluorescent rolonies. Existing spot-calling approaches can be conservative where signals overlap, while supervised deep learning is limited by the lack of reliable manual ground truth in real tissue images. Here we present PhySeqNet, a physics-informed deep learning framework for annotation-free fluorescent foci detection in BARseq. PhySeqNet trains U-Net detectors entirely on semi-synthetic images generated from an instrument-matched optical model combined with real sample-free experimental noise, and is integrated into pyBARseq, a modular Python pipeline for BARseq analysis. PhySeqNet achieved high detection performance on held-out simulated data across wavelength bands. On real tissue images, where ground truth is unavailable, we evaluated detections by forward-model reconstruction: PhySeqNet with conservative barcode-aware non-maxima suppression (NMSB) achieved higher reconstruction fidelity (NCC and MS-SSIM) than the BarDensr single-shot estimator, tuned classical spot detectors, and a pretrained deep-learning detector. In the analyzed brain section, PhySeqNet with NMSB yielded a median of 51 counts per cell versus 47 for BarDensr, with a similar number of genes detected per cell. The recovered transcripts produced spatial expression patterns qualitatively consistent with Allen MERFISH reference data and preserved cell-type composition after scANVI label transfer. These results show that physics-informed simulation can train practical, annotation-free detectors that improve BARseq sensitivity without disrupting downstream biological interpretation.
one_liner: PhySeqNet uses physics-informed synthetic training data to detect fluorescent foci in BARseq without manual annotations.
why_it_matters: It improves spatial transcriptomics sensitivity while preserving downstream biological interpretation in dense tissue images.

title: Locality-Preparation Time Tradeoffs in Dissipative Quantum Systems
abstract: Dissipative state preparation engineers quantum many-body states as steady states of an open-system dynamics. The spatial range of the required dissipation sets both the feasibility of analog implementations and the connectivity and control complexity of digital ones. Yet how this locality quantitatively constrains preparation times remains largely unknown. Here, we establish an exact locality-preparation time relation for quadratic fermionic systems and develop a construction that optimizes the locality of the dissipative dynamics while preserving the target state. Applied to the Kitaev chain, our framework reveals sharply different locality-preparation time tradeoffs in critical and gapped regimes. At criticality, suppressing the algebraic tails of the jump operators necessarily forces the preparation time to grow algebraically with system size. By contrast, both trivial and topological gapped phases admit exponentially localized dissipation with a finite preparation time in the thermodynamic limit. Our results identify when fast dissipative preparation is compatible with local control and when criticality imposes an unavoidable dynamical cost.
one_liner: Derives locality-time tradeoffs for dissipative preparation of quadratic fermionic steady states, with sharp Kitaev-chain contrasts.
why_it_matters: It clarifies when local dissipation can prepare many-body states quickly and when criticality forces slow dynamics.

title: Replica Transition at Measurement-Altered Ising Criticality
abstract: Performing measurements on gapless quantum ground states can give rise to new universal phenomena, whose origins remain poorly understood even for the paradigmatic Ising critical point. Replica methods offer a natural framework to study such post-measurement ensembles, with the replica limit $Q\to 1$ describing physical Born-averaged observables. Here we show that, for the monitored critical Ising chain, the replicated post-measurement ensemble of states itself undergoes a phase transition precisely at the physically relevant replica limit $Q \to 1$, preventing standard replica treatments. We use boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) methods to explain the underlying mechanism of this transition. Our methods yield a perturbative analytic calculation of the universal $O(1)$ constant in the Shannon entropy of the measurement record, previously known only numerically. We also apply our tools to study measurement-averaged spin correlators, providing a unified description of the universal properties of measurement outcomes and post-measurement states in the critical Ising chain.
one_liner: Shows a replica transition at the physical Q->1 limit for measurement-altered Ising criticality using BCFT tools.
why_it_matters: It exposes a fundamental obstacle for standard replica methods in monitored critical systems.

title: Diversity-Aware Ensemble of Quantum-Classical Models via Combinatorial Fusion
abstract: Variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are highly sensitive to circuit architecture, yet most quantum machine learning pipelines select a single best design and discard the remaining candidates. This paper addresses whether the structural diversity across quantum circuit search spaces can be used to produce stronger predictions through model fusion. We apply Combinatorial Fusion Analysis (CFA), a model fusion framework that selects and combines multiple scoring systems using rank-score function (RSF) and cognitive diversity (CD), to a pool of 29 architecturally diverse classical models and quantum circuits. Using a diversity-aware model selection method, we identify subsets of maximally diverse models and combine them with both score and rank combination. Experiments on four binary classification benchmarks covering different domains demonstrate that CFA-based hybrid classical-quantum fusion consistently outperform the best individual model on every dataset considered with improvements up to 6.03% in accuracy. When comparing with relevant literatures, the CFA framework further achieves superior performance across all four datasets.
one_liner: Uses combinatorial fusion to combine diverse quantum and classical models for improved binary classification.
why_it_matters: It suggests quantum ML pipelines can benefit from preserving architectural diversity instead of selecting one circuit.

title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Generated suites almost always execute, but discrimination lags behind: the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval, so executability alone overstates test quality. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. QTestBench offers a reproducible, cross-framework benchmark for the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.
one_liner: Introduces QTestBench to evaluate whether LLM-generated quantum tests distinguish correct code from faulty solutions.
why_it_matters: It gives a more trustworthy benchmark for quantum code testing than executability alone.

title: A Hardware-Native Trapped-Ion Hybrid Qudit-Oscillator Instruction Set
abstract: Scaling trapped-ion processors by adding ions remains challenging. A complementary route exploits the multilevel internal structure of each ion to increase the computational Hilbert space per ion. We introduce a hardware-native hybrid qudit-oscillator instruction set for a general d-level internal register coupled to bosonic modes and prove that three of its native operation families suffice for universality of one qudit coupled to several modes. Adding an entangling operation between ions extends universality to a connected register of several qudits. The architecture natively supports both phase-space and sideband instruction sets and is implemented in the open-source framework HybridLane. As a representative application, we reproduce the dissipative vibronic dynamics of a three-chromophore complex previously simulated on a hybrid qubit-oscillator superconducting platform. Moving from a one-qubit-per-state register to a single qudit stores the entire electronic manifold in one ion, so every electronic coupling becomes a local intra-ion transition and the lab-frame Hamiltonian compiles directly into the ISA. Under the stated sequential timing model from a 40Ca+ qudit processor, one Trotter step is projected to run about ten times faster on the qudit, with an average RMSE of approximately 1.1 percent against the published reference.
one_liner: Proposes a trapped-ion hybrid qudit-oscillator instruction set and implements it in the HybridLane framework.
why_it_matters: It expands trapped-ion compilation beyond qubits by exploiting multilevel ions and motional modes natively.

title: No advantage from classical assistance for energy-constrained bosonic dephasing channels
abstract: We prove that four capacities of single-mode bosonic dephasing channels coincide under an average photon-number constraint: the unassisted quantum capacity, the unassisted private capacity, the two-way classically assisted quantum capacity, and the two-way public-classically assisted private capacity. The assistance may be interactive: the parties can exchange classical messages between channel uses and choose subsequent inputs based on earlier outcomes. For every finite value of the constraint, their common value is the coherent information optimized over Fock-diagonal input states satisfying the constraint. The proof uses a relative entropy comparison with the completely dephasing channel to derive chain rules for the Rains relative entropy and the relative entropy of entanglement. These chain rules give an upper bound on the rates achievable by adaptive protocols whose mean input photon number is constrained on average over all channel uses. We also show that both chain rules are attained by canonical purifications of finite-energy Fock-diagonal states.
one_liner: Proves classical assistance does not increase several energy-constrained capacities of bosonic dephasing channels.
why_it_matters: It simplifies capacity theory for these channels by collapsing assisted and unassisted cases to one formula.

title: Statistical Optical Replication and Mixing of Spatial Information across Wavelengths
abstract: Accessing and combining the spatial information carried by light at different wavelengths is important for linking structured-light encoding with spectrally distinct detection channels. Here, we introduce a correlation-enabled linear-optical framework for cross-wavelength imaging, bidirectional replication, and spatial information mixing. Shared random holographic modulation establishes correlations between nondegenerate optical fields, allowing spatial information to be retrieved from joint intensity fluctuations. In the demonstrated replicator, a spatial pattern encoded at one wavelength is read out in the detection coordinates of another through intensity correlations. Selecting diffraction-order pairs produces correlation kernels containing either the product or the conjugate product of two input field envelopes. These operations reproduce the spatial algebra underlying sum- and difference-frequency generation, while the optical fields retain their original carrier frequencies. The theory accounts for wavelength-dependent propagation and coordinate scaling, linking the input structures to observable correlation patterns. Together, these results establish a common framework for cross-wavelength spatial information processing through engineered optical correlations and joint detection.
one_liner: Presents a correlation-enabled optical method for replicating and mixing spatial information across wavelengths.
why_it_matters: It offers linear-optical access to cross-wavelength spatial processing without changing carrier frequencies.

title: Bicycle Race: small two-block codes on the Pareto frontier
abstract: Two-block group-algebra codes are among the simplest quantum LDPC codes, and many of them are translation invariant on a twisted torus, which suits neutral-atom arrays and other platforms with movable qubits. We ask how far they go at small sizes when searched systematically across all groups. To tackle this question, we use a series of algebraic constraints and screens to design a search pipeline capable of enumerating broad and complete swathes of two-block codes on a laptop. With it we census about $10^8$ two-block codes with up to $320$ qubits at check weights five to nine. Several of these censuses are exhaustive, and support complete statements; for instance, the Gross code is, up to equivalence, the only abelian weight-six two-block code with $n \le 200$ to reach $kd^2/n=12$, and the known $[[64,18,8]]$ is the best two-block code by $kd^2/n$ across weights five to nine with $n \le 94$. The censuses are also large enough to give insights into where good codes live - they concentrate in a handful of groups; abelian groups give the best codes at small $n$ and non-abelian groups at large $n$, with the crossover appearing to move out as the check weight grows; and high quality codes become $100$ to $1000$ times rarer per draw from weight six to weights eight and nine. Using the group algebra and the census data to steer a statistical search finds four to fifteen times as many good codes as uniform draws in equal time. Among the codes found are $[[102,20,10]]$ and $[[120,24,10]]$ at check weight nine, which we simulate in noisy syndrome-extraction circuits, and $[[288,16,16]]$, the best weight-six two-block code with $n \le 300$. At check weights seven to nine, our best codes exceed the best published $kd^2/n$ with exact distance at the same check weight in most length bands up to $320$ qubits. All codes are available in a public database.
one_liner: Systematically searches small two-block quantum LDPC codes and identifies many Pareto-frontier candidates.
why_it_matters: It maps where high-quality small LDPC codes appear and provides a database for hardware-oriented code design.

title: An Annealing-based Quantum Neural Network with Discrete Wavelet Transforms for Enhanced Air Pollution Nowcasting
abstract: Air pollution poses a significant threat to public health, exacerbated by the rapid industrialization and urbanization of modern society. While traditional deep learning offers predictive capabilities, recent advancements in quantum machine learning (QML) present a compelling alternative. Here, we introduce a scalable hybrid framework that integrates variational quantum circuits with quantum annealing. Leveraging a neuromorphic quantum computing platform to transcend the qubit limitations of the NISQ era, we model particulate matter (PM$_{2.5}$) dynamics using high-density urban data from the UK. We demonstrate that our Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) exhibit an intrinsic resilience to input volatility, significantly outperforming classical baselines (MLP and LSTM) on raw, high-entropy environmental data. Furthermore, we successfully scaled the model to 172 qubits, observing a synergistic enhancement when coupled with wavelet decomposition that achieves state-of-the-art predictive fidelity. These findings establish a critical benchmark for quantum utility, proving that scalable, neuromorphic quantum machine learning can now address complex, non-linear real-world problems.
one_liner: Combines annealing-based quantum neural networks with wavelet transforms for PM2.5 nowcasting on urban data.
why_it_matters: It tests scalable quantum ML on a noisy real-world environmental forecasting task.

title: Maximally antiflat fixed-particle-number fermionic states
abstract: Fermionic Gaussian states are completely characterized by their two-point correlations, making the covariance matrix a natural reference for quantifying non-Gaussian structure. Motivated by fermionic antiflatness, we study its extremal form for pure number-conserving states and ask which states can be maximally antiflat and how they can be constructed. We show that, at fixed particle number, maximal first antiflatness is equivalent to a completely flat one-body reduced density matrix, and we obtain a complete existence classification together with explicit block and cyclic-orbit constructions of all allowed sectors. We then investigate the structure that appears beyond the covariance level. Maximally antiflat states with identical one-body data can exhibit distinct connected four-point correlations, which we characterize through the four-point Majorana Wick error and, equivalently, the connected two-body reduced density matrix cumulant. We show that this quartic structure is necessarily nonzero and formulate its extremization as a two-body reduced density matrix (2RDM) purity problem. Combining this framework with a Hilbert--Schmidt estimate of Christiansen for truncated two-body correlations, we obtain an upper bound on the connected quartic structure in terms of first antiflatness. Our results establish both a complete characterization of maximal fermionic antiflatness at fixed particle number and a constrained hierarchy linking covariance-level flatness to higher-order non-Gaussian correlations.
one_liner: Classifies maximally antiflat fixed-particle-number fermionic states and links flat covariance to higher correlations.
why_it_matters: It sharpens how non-Gaussian fermionic structure appears beyond one-body data.

title: Quantum Query Complexity of Maximum Degree and its Generalizations
abstract: We study the quantum query complexity of several basic graph problems. 1) We prove a tight $Θ(n^{3/2})$ bound for finding a maximum-out-degree vertex in an $n$-vertex tournament, resolving a conjecture of Mande, Paraashar, and Saurabh [FSTTCS'23]. 2) Using the same proof idea, we give a direct proof that finding a maximum-degree vertex in an $n$-vertex undirected graph requires $Θ(n^{3/2})$ quantum queries, a bound implicit in the work of Apers and Lee [CCC'21]. Both lower bounds above hold even for computing only the maximum degree or maximum out-degree. 3) We also study Maximum $(k,n-k)$-Cut, which asks for the largest cut with one side of size $k$. For every constant $k\geq 1$, we give an $O(n^{2-1/(k+1)})$-query quantum algorithm. 4) We establish a reduction to Maximum $(k,n-k)$-Cut involving $k$-Graph Collision, which asks whether the marked vertices of a known graph contain a $k$-clique. For $k\geq 3$, this yields unconditional lower bounds with exponents strictly larger than $3/2$, showing that this problem is strictly harder than computing maximum degree. Additionally, under a conjecture we propose for $k$-Graph Collision, the reduction yields a lower bound matching our upper bound above.
one_liner: Establishes tight and generalized quantum query bounds for maximum-degree and related graph problems.
why_it_matters: It resolves a tournament maximum-degree conjecture and separates harder cut-like graph queries.

title: A scalable sample-based quantum diagonalization solver for general Pauli-sum Hamiltonians
abstract: A scalable ground-state solver to be used in sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) is presented. The solver is built on JAX API, and is intended to be run on GPU platforms and possibly many-GPU high-performance computing facilities. It is capable of subspace diagonalization in up to $2^{30}$-dimensional subspace, with possible upgrades to enable even larger-scale operations. The two main components, a general-purpose eigensolver and an SQD-specific matrix-vector operation function, are described in detail. Efficiency of the eigensolver with respect to the GPU memory is demonstrated using a simple physics model. Furthermore, good strong scaling of the eigensolver in many-GPU environment is observed.
one_liner: Presents a JAX/GPU solver for sample-based quantum diagonalization of general Pauli-sum Hamiltonians.
why_it_matters: It targets scalable SQD workflows by enabling very large subspace diagonalization on GPU systems.

title: A Warped Born Rule Turns an Observer into a Maxwell's Demon
abstract: Quantum mechanics seems to be an incredibly delicate theory. Slight alterations to nearly any part of its structure can lead to huge qualitative differences and wildly unphysical predictions. Here, we explore the many-body consequences of replacing the Born rule $p(m)\propto\|P_m|ψ\rangle|^2$ by a warped rule $p_b(m)\propto\|P_m|ψ\rangle\|^{2b}$. Specifically, in systems with conserved particle number, evolution punctuated by repeated local particle observations acquires a probabilistic bias over measurement histories with an effect controlled by the sign of $b-1$. For $b>1$, this bias generically drives the gas to collect into nearly frozen configurations. Similar to the action of Maxwell's demon, the simple act of observation seems to extract entropy from a closed system. For $b<1$, the bias is reversed, generically scouring out long-wavelength fluctuations to produce a hyperuniform gas. We study this effect in a one-dimensional quantum gas, where these two phases are derived analytically for a particular measurement scheme and corroborated numerically for more general procedures with discrete-time projective-measurement circuit models using matrix product state simulations. We additionally discuss how this bias manifests in a common technique that often employs this warped rule, the ``replica trick,'' implying qualitative differences between finite-replica and replica-limit calculations.
one_liner: Shows that a nonlinear “warped” Born rule can bias repeated measurements into frozen clumps or hyperuniform gases.
why_it_matters: It sharpens how tiny deviations from quantum measurement rules can create unphysical thermodynamic behavior.
